Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
1152 AM MDT Thu Aug 27 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Thunderstorm coverage decreases Thursday and Friday with mainly
  isolated high-based showers/storms with gusty winds.

- Temperatures return to the 90s Friday andSaturday across the 
  plains.

- Thunderstorm coverage increases for late Saturday and Sunday. 

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Wednesday/...
Issued at 228 AM MDT Thu Aug 27 2026

Throughout the day today, the axis of the upper level ridge will 
shift east over Colorado, allowing warmer air to advect into the 
region. 700-mb temperatures should reach up to 15-17 dg C which 
roughly translates to temperatures in the high 80s to low 90s 
across the plains. With the upper level ridge shifting eastward, 
we will also start drying out over most the forecast area. This, 
combined with warming aloft, will result in less thunderstorm 
activity this afternoon, although CAMs still favor a few storms 
developing over the Front Range and spilling onto the adjacent 
plains. Given less moisture availability, main concerns for any 
storm over the mountains and I-25 Corridor will be strong outflow
winds. 

There is also a conditional threat for severe thunderstorms over the 
far northeastern plains later in the afternoon/evening hours. Models 
hint at a weak 700-mb shortwave north/northeast of Colorado, 
which should provide forcing for thunderstorm activity over 
Nebraska. While CAMs keep most of the storms out of Colorado 
(with the 06Z runs less aggressive with thunderstorm activity 
compared to the 00Z runs), can't rule out an isolated storm 
developing over the far northeastern plains (10-20% chance), 
especially since that area will be able to hang onto the low-level
moisture and thus have better instability throughout the day. 
Given MLCAPE values up to 1000-1500 J/kg and 0-6 Km bulk shear of
40 kts, storms would be capable of producing hail and strong 
winds. 

Warmer temperatures arrive by Friday and Saturday as the upper 
level ridge continues shifting eastward, with highs reaching the 
low-to- mid 90s both days. A strong upper level low over the 
Pacific Northwest will cause flow aloft to increase and turn 
west/southwest over Colorado. This will create breezy conditions 
over the high terrain, but also re-introduce mid-level moisture 
into the region. On Friday, we could see isolated high-based 
showers and thunderstorms. But, Saturday afternoon looks better 
for thunderstorm activity. Convection should be high-based, with 
only a few storms producing beneficial rainfall. 

Towards the end of the weekend/beginning of next week, the upper 
level low will trek across the U.S./Canada border, with embedded 
shortwaves moving over Colorado. "Cooler" temperatures (if you 
consider 80s to be cooler) will arrive, along with better low- 
level moisture. Ensemble guidance continues to favor storms 
Sunday and Monday, but looks to have backed off for Tuesday due to
an exiting shortwave. This could still change depending on the 
evolution of the multiple disturbances, so will keep an eye on it.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Friday/...
Issued at 1145 AM MDT Thu Aug 27 2026

VFR conditions are expected through this TAF package. Isolated
showers and thunderstorms are expected this afternoon. However,
due to the lower coverage and increased uncertainly in impacts to
the airports, we've left any mention of showers in the PROB30 for 
this afternoon and early evening. Showers will have the potential
for weak dry microbursts and gusty winds at all 3 TAF sites.
Models are showing some showers lingering after the initial 
round, so we'e pushed the PROB30 for a few extra hours, so it's 
now 22Z to 03Z at KDEN and KAPA and 21Z to 02Z at KBJC. Winds 
overnight will turn more towards drainage, becoming westerly by 
mid morning tomorrow. 

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
1130 AM MDT Fri Aug 28 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Isolated/scattered high based showers/storms Friday with gusty 
  winds. 

- Temperatures return to the 90s Friday and Saturday across the
  plains.

- Thunderstorm coverage increases for late Saturday through
  Monday.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Thursday/...
Issued at 137 AM MDT Fri Aug 28 2026

An upper level ridge remains centered near the Arizona/New Mexico
border early this morning, leaving most of Colorado in weak
wester/northwesterly flow aloft. This ridge is expected to slowly
shift eastward over the next several days with few other synoptic
scale features of note. 

The plume of better monsoon moisture will remain well off to the
west and northwest today. Modest mid-level moisture combined with
deep mixing will lead to widely scattered showers and
thunderstorms this afternoon, though most of the convection should
be weak given only meager instability. Most forecast soundings
show inverted-V profiles across most of the I-25 corridor, and
gusty outflow winds will be the main hazard this afternoon and
evening. Meanwhile, it'll be another hot day today as 700mb
temperatures climb back to 16-18C. High temperatures should reach
the low to mid 90s across most of the lower elevations.

Saturday features more of the same, with the flow aloft backing to
the west-southwest. Models generally try to increase moisture
aloft a bit, with precipitable water values settling near an inch
across most of the I-25 corridor, with more anomalous PW across
northern/northwestern Colorado. Guidance generally tries to
develop a more organized band of showers and thunderstorms close
to the Wyoming border, associated with a weak mid-level shortwave
and cold front. The ECMWF remains a bit more bullish with this
potential compared to the rest of tonight's guidance, though even
the more aggressive solutions don't have much in the way of
rainfall outside of the northern mountains/North Park.

Moisture increases a little bit more on Sunday, with another weak
shortwave racing through the southwesterly flow aloft. Surface
moisture will remain a limiting factor with dew points in the 40s
leading to meager CAPE values across most of the forecast area.
Another, perhaps better defined shortwave moves through on Monday
and will likely provide our best chance of rainfall, though sfc
moisture/instability will again be a bit of a question mark.

By mid-week, most of the remaining moisture aloft sinks off to the
south, meaning that near/above normal temperatures and generally
dry conditions are forecast through the rest of the period. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Saturday/...
Issued at 1122 AM MDT Fri Aug 28 2026

Expect sct high based showers with an isold tstm possible between 
20z and 00z. Brief gusts up to 40 mph will certainly be possible.
After 00z, coverage of showers should diminish and end around 02z.
Winds will gradually become more NW/N by 21z and then switch to 
more NNE by 00z. Winds this evening will switch to SE/S by 02z 
and then SSW by 05z.

On Sat, winds will become more WSW by 16z. Any high based
showers/tstms should hold off until after 18z.


&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
1200 PM MDT Sat Aug 29 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Warm again today, with increased chances of showers and
  thunderstorms this afternoon and evening.

- Active monsoon pattern continues Sunday and Monday.

- Warm and dry pattern returns for most of next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Friday/...
Issued at 212 AM MDT Sat Aug 29 2026

Water vapor satellite imagery suggests that the plume of deeper
monsoon moisture is slowly approaching our forecast area tonight,
with broad southwesterly flow aloft to the north of a slowly
weakening ridge. 

Today will see more scattered showers and thunderstorms, with a
bit more coverage compared to yesterday. A slight increase in
boundary layer moisture along with slightly cooler mid-level
temperatures will lead to a modest increase in instability for the
afternoon, and convective initiation will likely be aided by a
sagging mid-level front this afternoon and evening. Both the HREF
and REFS suggest widely scattered thunderstorms developing by the
early afternoon, and at least a few showers and storms are likely
to linger through most of the evening and early overnight hours
(especially closer to the front).

The plume of monsoon moisture isn't expected to move much on
Sunday. The lack of synoptic forcing will likely limit storm
coverage across the plains, but scattered showers and storms
are forecast across the high country during the afternoon hours. 

A more pronounced shortwave is expected to move through the region
on Monday or Monday night, leading to an increase in storm
coverage across most of the state. Recent models are a little too
slow with this wave for most of our forecast area to benefit from
the increased synoptic scale ascent, with better chances for
precipitation off to the south and west of our CWA. Still, widely
scattered showers/storms are forecast again, perhaps lingering
through most of the overnight hours across the plains where
the environment would support elevated convection.

Moisture quickly diminishes by Tuesday as the ridge continues to
weaken and push off to the east. The latter half of the week looks
rather quiet with the ridge restrengthening over the southeastern
CONUS, before slowly drifting back towards the region as we
approach next weekend. High temperatures should approach 90F
across the plains most days, with a gradual warming trend likely
by this time next week.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Sunday/...
Issued at 1155 AM MDT Sat Aug 29 2026

Winds have been rather variable and under 10 kts this morning, but
will start to settle in a more westerly direction over the next
few hours. Another windy/stormy afternoon remains likely at all 
three sites this afternoon and evening with the possibility for 
multiple waves of high-based showers and thunderstorms. A TEMPO 
group is in place starting at 20z to cover this. DCAPE values 
could reach around 1300 J/kg this afternoon translating into wind 
gusts in excess of 35 kts even if a shower is only nearby and does
not necessarily pass directly over the location. 

There could be a brief lull in the early evening, but showers and
thunderstorms remain possible through this evening. An outflow 
boundary/pseudo-front is most likely around 2-4z with some 
additional showers/thunderstorms possible and winds from the north
with gusts in excess of 35 kts possible once again.

Winds are expected to turn to drainage tonight after the showers
subside. By tomorrow morning, winds will start to turn clockwise 
to NNW for the afternoon. We have introduced a PROB30 starting at
20z tomorrow for the possibility of high-based showers and 
thunderstorms bringing similar wind gusts to this afternoon.

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
538 AM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Active monsoon pattern continues Sunday and Monday.

- Warm and dry pattern returns for most of the upcoming week.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Saturday/...
Issued at 1222 AM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

There haven't been too many significant changes in the large scale
pattern over the last 24 hours. A broad upper ridge remains
centered over the south central CONUS, with a trough noted over
the northern Rockies... leaving the area in broad southwesterly
flow aloft. This also puts us square in the middle of the
monsoonal moisture, and there's been a good amount of
precipitation falling across northwestern Colorado, which has
spread as far east as Grand/Jackson county.

Overnight CAMs are actually in decent agreement in how today's
convective potential plays out. Most guidance pushes a cluster of
showers and thunderstorms across Middle/North Park late this
morning into the early afternoon, which then advances east into
the Front Range and I-25 corridor by early/mid afternoon. The
convective environment is marginally favorable across most of the
lower elevations, with modest MLCAPE (~500 J/kg) but increased
deep layer shear. We can't totally rule out a few strong to severe
wind gusts with any stronger showers/storms as convection
continues to push eastward through the afternoon and evening
hours.

Monday still looks to feature the best chance of precipitation
across most of our forecast area, as a more pronounced shortwave
races across the state during the afternoon/early overnight hours.
There's timing differences across the various models, but
reasonably good agreement that a convective cluster will develop
across southwestern Colorado during the day, advancing into our
forecast area by the mid/late afternoon hours. Like the past few
days, meager surface/boundary layer moisture will limit
instability, but the stronger synoptic forcing should lead to more
widespread rainfall into Monday evening/Monday night. 

By Tuesday, the center of the 500mb ridge should slide east into 
the Ohio Valley, while a strong closed low spins off the coast of 
British Columbia. Across the region, southwesterly flow aloft will
persist. Moisture will diminish through this timeframe, with 
enough drying by Wednesday and Thursday that only a couple of 
weak showers are in the forecast across the the high country. 

The forecast pattern becomes a bit more complex as we approach
next weekend. The closed low near the Pacific Northwest coastline 
will eventually drift onshore, and its approach towards our area
should lead to a more poleward component of the mid/upper level
winds. Further complicating the pattern is the potential tropical
cyclone development across the eastern Pacific, which could
contribute to additional tropical moisture advection into the
region by next weekend. There is a fairly large spread across the
overnight guidance and it'll likely be a while until we have a
better handle on things, but the overall pattern would suggest
that we'll see precipitation chances increase towards the end of
our forecast period.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z TAFS through 12Z Monday/...
Issued at 528 AM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

VFR conditions are expected through the TAF period. Main concern
through tonight is the potential for one or two clusters of
convection to bring variable/gusty outflow winds this afternoon
into the early evening hours.

Light drainage flow should turn clockwise through the morning
hours with speeds remaining generally light. Most guidance brings
a cluster of SHRA/TSRA through the terminals between about 20-02z.
There's a little more moisture/instability compared to the last
couple days and, but outflow winds are more likely than direct TS
impacts. A few showers may linger beyond 00z with winds quickly
turning to the southeast, with drainage likely establishing by
around 06z.  

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Monday/...

Radar as of 1745z shows a broken line of showers and 
thunderstorms moving through Grand, Jackson, and western Larimer 
counties. Based on the latest radar trends and CAMs, have kept a 
TEMPO and VCSH starting at 20z (adjusted KBJC to start at 19z) 
for the possibility of high-based showers and thunderstorms for 
much of the afternoon. These could bring gusty outflow winds in 
excess of 35 kts, rain, and briefly lowering ceilings. There is a 
~30-40% chance that showers and thunderstorms linger through about
4z this evening. Behind the convection, winds should turn to 
drainage rather quickly... as early as 4z.

Winds should turn clockwise to north-northeast to northeast by 
early tomorrow afternoon. Tomorrow will be another day with a 
TEMPO and VCSH starting at 20z for similar threats- gusty outflow winds
in excess of 35 kts, rain, and briefly lowering ceilings. Ceilings
could briefly drop to around 7000 feet AGL given more mid-level 
moisture is expected to be present. A PRO30 or TEMPO will likely 
be needed past 0z Tuesday in the next update.

National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
148 PM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Scattered showers and storms capable of producing strong to
  severe wind gusts are expected to continue through the evening. 

- Better precipitation chances on Monday, with another round of
  afternoon/evening showers and storms, a few may become severe.

- Warmer and drier conditions expected from Tuesday onward. 
  


&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Sunday/...
Issued at 124 PM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Current radar shows storms are making their way off the northern 
Front Range early this afternoon, with another round moving across 
the Continental Divide. The primary hazard with today's showers and 
storms will, once again, be strong outflow winds. So far, storms 
have been producing a few tenths of rainfall and wind gusts between 
40 to 50 mph. Storms have been moving between 30-40 kts, which will 
help keep flash flooding concerns limited, but if we do see any back-
building, there is enough moisture in place to see some heavy 
downpours, mainly across the higher elevations. While today's 
instability is expected to be slightly increased over Saturday, it
remains fairly weak, with only a few hundred to roughly 500 J/kg 
of MLCAPE observed on the SPC mesoanalysis. CAMs continue to be in
decent agreement about high-based storms/showers continuing their
trek eastward across the plains through the afternoon and 
evening. These will be capable of producing strong outflow winds, 
with at least a few severe wind gusts possible. Current 
temperature readings show roughly a ten degree difference from 
this time yesterday, with today's afternoon highs forecast to run 
a few degrees cooler than yesterday. 

Southwesterly flow aloft will continue to usher monsoonal moisture 
into Colorado on Monday. Given the increased moisture, proximity to 
the right entrance of a 500 mb jet, and the aid of lift from an 
approaching shortwave sometime in the afternoon/evening, this will 
be our best chance for precipitation across the forecast area 
with this wave of monsoonal moisture. CAMs continue to show a 
cluster of storms move through the Four Corners Monday morning, 
pushing northeast across Colorado through the day. We could see a 
few stronger to severe storms in the afternoon, with the CAMs 
honing in on the better instability being along and east of the 
Palmer Divide (as high as ~1200 J/kg of MLCAPE). Given the better 
moisture, we will have a better chance for some localized heavier 
rainfall amounts, but with the mean flow aloft roughly moving 
35-40 kts, this should help limit flash flood potential. 
Additionally, with DCAPE ranging from 1200-1500 J/kg across the 
plains, generally east of the urban corridor, the primary threat 
will be with gusty outflows once again, but with increasing 0-6 km
bulk shear, we may see some marginally severe hail with some of 
the stronger storms. Depending on the timing of the shortwave, we 
could see showers/storms linger late into the night. Near normal 
temperatures are expected across the forecast area. 

Southwesterly flow aloft will remain in place through the week as 
the upper-level ridge persists over the eastern US. Monsoonal 
moisture is expected to continue flowing into the region, but 
amounts are expected to diminish for a few days midweek, as the 
higher amounts should stay to our southeast. Things in the Pacific 
look to become active over this period, from a parade of storms 
moving towards Hawaii, to a fairly strong closed low dropping south 
along the West Coast. Depending on how these features interact, we 
could see some more active weather return by late in the week, but 
for now, the forecast calls for slightly less convection each 
afternoon after Monday, with near normal temperatures on Tuesday, 
gradually warming through the end of the work-week.  

&&

.AVIATION /00Z TAFS through 00Z Tuesday/...
Issued at 545 PM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Radar as of 2345z is rather quiet across the Denver metro after 
an afternoon of showers, thunderstorms, and gusty winds at all 
three sites. CAMs continue to suggest the possibility of 
additional high-based showers and thunderstorms either moving off 
the Palmer Divide or the higher terrain to the west this evening 
through 5z. These could bring gusty outflow winds in excess of 35 
kts and briefly lowering ceilings. Behind the convection, winds 
will shift to drainage through Monday morning.

Winds should turn clockwise to north-northeast or even east by 
early tomorrow afternoon. Have continued to refine the timing of 
showers/thunderstorms for tomorrow afternoon and evening based on 
the latest CAMs. A TEMPO and VCTS starts at 21z (20z for KAPA) for
similar threats to today- gusty outflow winds in excess of 35 
kts and briefly lowering ceilings. Ceilings could briefly drop to
around 7000 feet AGL given more mid-level moisture than today is 
expected to be present. A PROB30 is in place for tomorrow evening 
with additional rounds of SHRA/TSRA possible. Timing of the 
SHRA/TSRA will continue to be refined in future updates.

and evening. In fact, showers and thunderstorms are already ongoing 
across the Four Corners region and Southwest CO as of 1pm. At the

instability lacking across our area, which could limit the severe 
potential, especially for the I-25 urban corridor and adjacent 
plains.

to 50 mph as DCAPE is expected to be around 1000 J/kg. MLCAPE is 
forecast to reach around 1000 J/kg, mainly for the far eastern 
plains. 0-6 km bulk shear should be about 30 to 40 kts with the 
greatest shear expected in our eastern plains where temperatures 
have warmed into the mid 80s as of 12pm. Therefore, a low risk for 
hail of 1 to perhaps 1.5 inches in diameter exists for the far 
eastern plains. There is also a low flood threat given that the 
ingredients are in place, but storm motion should be rather quick 
this afternoon with mean wind around 30-40 kts- limiting the overall 
threat. A decent moist vertical profile for the area means PWATs of 
150-175% of average for this time of year. Thus, burn scars, areas 
where storms linger, and locations that receive multiple rounds of 
heavy rainfall today would be most susceptible to minor flooding. 
The warm cloud layer depth is relatively shallow, further limiting 
the flooding threat.

CAMs are in decent agreement that there will be at least two rounds 
of showers and storms this afternoon and evening. Showers and storms 
should overspread the southern high country as early as 2-3pm. The 
most widespread showers for the high country and Urban Corridor 
should be between about 4pm and 8pm. These should then push off to 
the north and east. An additional round or two of showers and storms 
is possible for the evening and overnight hours through about 2am 
tomorrow morning. Tonight, some low clouds and patchy fog are 
possible for the plains following the rain. Some light rain showers 
could linger into tomorrow morning for the plains, though the odds 
are rather low. 

High temperatures for today and tomorrow will be near average- in 
the mid 80s for the plains. Some isolated storms are possible for 
the high country and areas south and east of Denver tomorrow 
afternoon. There will likely be a low threat for severe weather near 
the Palmer Divide with any storms that could form, but moisture and 
lift will be lacking compared to today. The high pressure shifts off 
to the mid-Atlantic and Southern US shutting off the monsoonal 
moisture feed into our area by Wednesday. High temperatures will 
return to above average- in the mid 80s and low 90s across the 
plains- for the end of the week and into the weekend. Little to no 
rainfall is expected through at least Friday.

By the weekend, south to southwest flow aloft could return. Moisture 
from a tropical disturbance in the Pacific could also be pulled into 
the Western US, but as of now the deepest moisture looks to miss our 
area to the west. Thus, the highest rainfall chances should stay 
confined to the high country until Sunday or Monday.

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...A cool and wet start to meteorological fall. Some 
rain could be heavy, leading to poor drainage flooding.

The backdoor cold front that pushed southwest of New England this 
morning starts to shift back to the northeast today, with increasing 
cloud cover this afternoon. As advertised the past several days, 
there are multiple rounds of beneficial rainfall this week, with the 
first round coming late tonight through Tuesday. With the frontal 
boundary shifting northeast, PWATs increase to between 1.8-2.0 
inches, interacting with a weak wave of low pressure riding along 
the boundary.

Timing-wise, rain aims to arrive around midnight west of the CT 
River Valley and around the time of the Tuesday morning commute for 
the I-95 corridor. Looking at BUFKIT, do see warm rain processes 
with the warm cloud layer around 10k feet. Locally heavy downpours, 
especially during the daytime Tuesday, are possible, which may lead 
to localized street and poor drainage flooding. This coincides with 
the Day 1-2 ERO Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for excessive 
rainfall.

Do think there will be a thin axis of heaviest rainfall across the 
southwest section of our CWA. Rainfall amounts are in the 
neighborhood of half an inch to an inch, with lesser amounts east of 
I-95, where totals are in the range of a quarter to half an inch. 
Since these are showers versus stratiform rain, there could be areas 
of higher and lower amounts within a relatively short distance. 
However, a subtle shift northeast could put some of the heaviest 
rainfall across parts of central Massachusetts and eastern 
Connecticut. Additionally, there's a lower chance for thunder, 
mainly Tuesday afternoon, with a few hundred J/kg of CAPE across 
mainly western Massachusetts and Connecticut, although it's not a 
significant risk.

Rain tapers off late Tuesday, with drier conditions overspreading 
the region Tuesday night into early Thursday morning. Given the 
clouds, expect a much cooler start to Tuesday, with highs mainly in 
the upper 60s to lower 70s. A true nod to the first day of 
meteorological fall.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Unsettled weather late Wed into Thursday, with 
several rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Low confidence on exact 
timing. 

1025 mb high pressure over the Maritimes should provide dry weather 
much of Wed, especially across eastern MA, while a frontal boundary 
lurks to the west and southwest of SNE. This front will eventually 
move northeast as a warm front later Wed and especially Wed night, 
resulting in an increased risk for showers and thunderstorms across 
SNE late Wed/Wed night. Cooler temps Wed, with 1025 Maritime high 
and ESE onshore flow, limiting max temps in the upper 60s and lower 
70s.

Trailing/secondary short wave and associated cold front impact the 
region around Thu. Potential for thunderstorms to become strong to 
severe during this time, as warm sector airmass overspreads SNE. 
However, better instability/higher theta-e airmass appears to remain 
southwest of SNE. Thus, potential for severe weather and flash 
flooding here looks limited at this time range. Heat and humidity 
return Thu with warm sector airmass, highs in the lower 80s and dew 
pts in the upper 60s and lower 70s. 

  
KEY MESSAGE 3...Improving weather Friday and into the holiday 
weekend. Other than a spot diurnal shower each day, dry weather 
prevails with a mix of clouds and sun. Cooler than normal with highs 
in the 70s and lows in the 50s, along with onshore breezes.

Definitely a sign of fall approaching, with robust northern stream 
Friday yielding a baroclinic 998 mb maritime low late Fri/Sat. This 
will yield a cool, brisk NE flow into the SNE over the weekend. 
Highs likely remaining in the 70s and overnight lows in the 50s. It 
will feel even cooler over southeast MA, including Cape Cod and the 
Islands, with northeast winds 15-25 mph. Cool cyclonic flow aloft 
will yield diurnal clouds each day and possibly a spot shower. 
Otherwise, dry weather prevails. Possibly warmer and less wind for 
Memorial Day Monday, as high amplitude trough moves offshore and 
1025 mb high settles over SNE.

strong 596DM upper ridge currently over the southern Plains and 
mid MS Valley area building eastward through the week becoming 
situated over the southern OH Valley and Carolinas by mid week 
then gradually weakening and beginning to slowly retrograde by 
the end of the week. This should result in strong subsidence 
over the region through the week with ensemble forecast 700mb 
temperatures at the 99th percentile with values around +10C.

increases confidence in the general lack of convection expected.

mid to late week suggesting a strong warming trend through the 
week with anomalously high temperatures (about 10 degrees above

high with EC EFI showing values around 0.7-0.8 and a nonzero 
shift of tails (similar to the max temperatures) with values 
about 5 to 10 degrees above normal. Southeast to southwesterly 
surface flow through the week will keep the low level moisture 
in place resulting in heat indices rising above 100 degrees all 
week and approaching heat advisory criteria mid to late week. 

KEY MESSAGE 2. Active weather and decreasing temperatures 
possible next weekend.

Ensembles and global guidance in good agreement showing the 
strong upper ridge retrograding westward back over the Plains 
states allowing for upper troughing along the East Coast next 
weekend. This should support slightly cooling temperatures and 
also allow shortwave energy to dive down the back side of the 
retreating ridge, bringing increased chances of rainfall back to
the forecast area. Rainfall will be welcomed again after a long
hot and generally dry week ahead.

evening with the main threat of locally heavy rainfall.

Stratus clouds have transitioned to a stratocumulus deck as 
daytime heating continues and temperatures rise through the 80s.

moderate instability as higher clouds are diminishing and more 
sun is expected. However, wind shear remains weak and organized 
convection is not anticipated. Hi-res guidance suggests isolated
convection through the afternoon into early evening favoring 
the eastern Midlands closer to the deeper moisture (PWATs around

vorticity). Due to slow storm motion and PWATs around 2 inches,

providing high rain rates.

the north of the Atlanta metro area. As the trough axis slowly 
continues towards the Atlantic coast, it will give the frontal 
boundary a push to the south. Low temperatures this morning will be 
in the mid to upper 60s in areas north of the boundary and in the 
low 70s in areas to the south. With the combination of wet soils 
soils from yesterday's rain, light winds, and ample low level 
moisture, patchy fog is expected during the early morning hours, 
most likely in areas along and south of I-85. As the frontal

concentrate moisture further south towards the Gulf. Areas of 
central and east Georgia will see precipitable water values of 2+ 
inches and dewpoints in the mid 70s while areas of northwest 
Georgia will see precipitable water values drop to between 
1.25-1.75 inches and dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s.

primarily along and south of the I-85 corridor where more ample 
moisture will remain. Higher coverage of storms and mostly cloudy 
skies will keep high temperatures limited to the upper 80s in 
central Georgia, though they will only rise into the low 90s in 
north Georgia. MUCAPE values are progged to peak between 1500-2500 
J/kg this afternoon. In portions of east Georgia, there is expected 
to be an overlap between this instability, strong low-level lapse 
rates, and high PWATs. This will favor an increased risk for a few 
severe storms capable of producing strong downburst winds, 
warranting a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) from the SPC. Stronger 
storms that occur will also be capable of producing locally heavy 
rain, with some isolated pockets of 3 or more inches where these

heavier rainfall will be most likely to the south of the fall line

front stalled across the area. Upper level flow will be weak over 
the Southeast on Saturday ahead of an approaching ridge set to build 
in over the region during the long term period. Southeasterly flow

forecast area and could drive the front back to the northwest.

upper 60s to low 70s and patchy fog during the early morning

unorganized, satellite imagery and buoy/oil rig observations show 
a closed circulation taking shape south of the Louisiana coast. 
Therefore, NHC indicates a TD or TS is likely to form today before
the system makes landfall on the Upper Texas coast tonight into 
Tuesday morning. Models generally bring the weakening system 
northwestward up the I-45 corridor into our southeast counties

as it runs into the upper ridge and drier air across North Texas 
from Wednesday night into Thursday.

timeframe in line with the latest NBM guidance. Model QPF is all

inches of rain with isolated higher amounts across our southeast

impact will be on temperatures. Increasing humidity alone would 
favor higher heat indices, but greater cloud cover and scattered 
convection should hold daytime temperatures several degrees lower 
across eastern portions of the area Wednesday. This competing 
influence is one reason confidence in heat headline coverage 
decreases after Tuesday despite the increasingly humid air mass.

slower solution would maintain clouds and scattered convection

temperatures across North and Central Texas. Most areas should 
return to predominantly dry conditions Friday into the weekend as

Although another hot summer day is expected across North and
Central Texas with highs in the upper 90s and lower 100s, the
approach of Tropical Storm Edouard will bring low rain chances
(10-30%) to the region this afternoon and evening. There are two 
primary reasons for the return of these lower rain chances:

1) The exceptionally moist tropical airmass associated with
Edouard will substantially increase the humidity above the
boundary layer. This will reduce the detrimental effects of
entrainment that has largely inhibited diurnally driven 
convection the last month. 

2) Forcing for ascent will move in with the approach of Edouard
as the mid-level vort max approaches North and Central Texas from
the southeast. While the amount of lift remains uncertain at this
time, at least weak forcing can be expected by this evening 
especially in the vicinity of the Brazos Valley.

Considering the two reasons above, very isolated showers (and
potentially a thunderstorm or two) can be expected across much of
North and Central Texas this afternoon and evening (10-20%
chance). Rain chances will be higher (20-30%) further southeast 
into the Brazos Valley in closer proximity to Edouard.

The most likely area to stay dry will be locations west of I-35
and north of I-20. Not only is this area furthest from the
localized lift associated with Edouard, but forecast soundings
continue to show much drier mid and upper-levels that will likely
inhibit the development of diurnally driven convection.

isolated coverage of showers and storms is expected across North

not break out of the 80s. As the remnants of Edouard slowly 
dissipate the latter half of this work week, temperatures will be 
slow to rebound wherever cloud cover and rain lingers. This will 
likely result in highs in the low and mid 90s for much of Central 
and Eastern Texas Wednesday through Friday.

Rainfall amounts are expected to be highest south of I-20 and east
of I-35. Rainfall totals through Friday will range from half an
inch to an inch for much of this area. However, localized areas
may see greater rainfall totals than this with locations in the 
Brazos Valley potentially seeing 2-3 inches of rain by Friday.

especially for any thunderstorms that can develop in the drier air

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Monday night)
Issued at 1220 PM CDT Fri Aug 28 2026

A comparatively quiet afternoon is shaping up across most of the 
area as drier mid and upper level air continues to work southward. 
Shallow cumulus has been developing with daytime heating, but radar 
remains quiet over land late this morning with convection confined 
to the coastal waters. The upper ridge currently centered over New 
Mexico will gradually shift east toward the Texas Panhandle through 
Saturday. While the ridge axis remains northwest of the CWA, enough 
subsidence and midlevel drying will extend into the area to suppress 
the typical late-August convective cycle. This should be especially 
true through much of the inland Louisiana parishes west of I-55 and 
north of I-10/12 corridors. Cannot completely eliminate convection 
given strong daytime heating and eventual development of the 
sea/lake breeze, but coverage should remain isolated this afternoon. 
The somewhat better moisture over far southeastern Louisiana and 
coastal Mississippi provides the best opportunity for a few storms, 
with the Mississippi coast favored relative to most inland locations.

Saturday looks quite similar. Continued dry air aloft and subsidence 
on the southeastern flank of the ridge should again keep most inland 
locations dry, with isolated convection primarily tied to the sea 
breeze and areas closer to the coast. Better coverage should remain 
over the coastal waters. With less convection and cloud cover, highs 
will climb into the lower to middle 90s. Peak heat indices should 
generally remain below advisory criteria through the weekend but 
still well into the 100s. Would probably be higher if not for some 
mixing down of dry air aloft.  

The pattern begins to change more noticeably Sunday as the upper 
ridge shifts farther north and east. This allows easterly flow to 
become better established across the northern Gulf while a weak 
inverted trough or other perturbation develops over the northeastern 
Gulf. The resulting moisture return should initially be most 
pronounced across the eastern and coastal portions of the CWA. 
Expect a meaningful increase in thunderstorm coverage Sunday from 
coastal Mississippi through southeast Louisiana, including the New 
Orleans metro, while the Baton Rouge area may remain on the western 
edge of the deeper moisture and see a somewhat smaller increase.
Increasing cloud cover and convection should hold temperatures down 
a couple degrees where storms become more numerous Sunday. Locally 
heavy rainfall and gusty winds will be possible with the stronger 
storms, but widespread heavy rainfall or severe weather is not 
currently anticipated.

MEFFER

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday through Thursday night)
Issued at 1220 PM CDT Fri Aug 28 2026

The primary story during the extended period will be the continued 
eastward tracking of the upper ridge and a corresponding increase in 
deep-layer moisture across the north-central Gulf Coast. Monday into 
Tuesday, the ridge center should be shifting toward the southern 
Appalachians, placing the local area firmly along its southern 
periphery. This favors persistent easterly to southeasterly flow 
from the Gulf and western Atlantic into the region. At the same 
time, the weak inverted trough moving west across the northern Gulf 
may provide an additional focus for convection. Rain chances should 
therefore remain elevated Monday and Tuesday, with the greatest 
coverage initially across coastal areas before better moisture 
spreads farther west and north.

Wednesday through Friday, the broad-scale pattern remains favorable 
for a progressively deeper tropical moisture profile. Guidance 
brings precipitable water values well above 2 inches, with some 
solutions approaching 2.5 inches late in the week. If that degree of 
moisture becomes established, convection should become increasingly 
efficient at producing heavy rainfall.

At this point there is not enough confidence in the location or 
persistence of convection to highlight a widespread flooding threat. 
However, the combination of deep tropical moisture, weak steering 
flow and repeated daily convection could eventually support 
localized heavy rainfall concerns, particularly during the latter 
half of the week if the wetter guidance verifies. This trend will 
need to be monitored as the moisture plume and any embedded Gulf 
circulations become better resolved.

Temperatures should remain close to late-August normals overall. 
Highs will generally reach the lower 90s, with upper 80s possible 
where convection develops earlier in the day and middle 90s possible 
where storms are delayed. There remains some potential for heat 
indices to approach advisory criteria, especially during the early 
to middle portion of the week in areas that remain dry through peak 
heating. However, the increasingly moist pattern does not 
automatically translate into a greater heat threat. While higher 
dewpoints favor larger heat indices, increasing cloud cover and 
thunderstorm coverage should increasingly limit afternoon 
temperatures. If the deeper tropical moisture arrives as currently 
expected late in the week, the duration and areal coverage of 108+ 
heat indices may actually decrease.

The largest uncertainty during the extended period remains the exact 
position of the upper ridge. A ridge axis displaced farther south or 
west would provide greater subsidence, reduce convective coverage 
and allow hotter temperatures. Conversely, a farther northeast ridge 
and stronger easterly moisture transport would favor greater 
thunderstorm coverage, heavier rainfall potential and somewhat 
cooler daytime temperatures.

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Wednesday night)
Issued at 1225 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Upper ridge centered north of Dallas this morning. An upper 
disturbance was off the southeast Louisiana coast to the south of 
Grand Isle. Surface high was over Virginia. Scattered showers and a 
few thunderstorms were rotating around the upper disturbance,
mainly over the coastal waters this morning, but are becoming 
more numerous over land this afternoon, mainly along and south of
the Interstate 10/12 corridor. Temperatures are approaching 90,
but probably won't get much higher than they are now. 

The disturbance over the Gulf is expected to drift slowly west or 
west-northwest over the next couple of days, likely reaching the 
upper Texas coast on Tuesday. Another disturbance will enter the 
eastern Gulf on Wednesday. Precipitable water values between 1.9 
and 2.1 inches are expected over much of the area through 
Wednesday. These are generally between the 75th and 90th 
percentile climatologically, and are more than sufficient to 
produce scattered to numerous showers and storms across the area. 
The best areal coverage is expected over the southern half of the 
area from the Interstate 10/12 corridor to the coast today and
again on Monday. The disturbance may be far enough away from the 
area Tuesday to limit areal coverage as compared to the next 36 
hours. Rainfall amounts each day will be highly variable, with 
only very limited areas getting heavy rainfall (> 1 inch). If
those spots of heavy rainfall occur over an urban area, they could
cause temporary problems, but widespread flooding issues are not
anticipated. Most of the precipitation should occur during the 
hours of maximum heating (afternoon), with much or all of the 
precipitation dissipating near or shortly after sunset each day.
The exception would be along immediate coastal areas, such as the
lower portions of the Louisiana coastal parishes, which could see
showers return near or before sunrise. 

Forecast soundings support highs in the 90 to 95 degree range 
through Wednesday. In most cases, those highs will be around midday 
or early afternoon, before convection becomes widespread. Areas 
that see convection develop early could even fall short of 90 
degrees each day. 

&&

(Thursday through Saturday night)
Issued at 1225 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

The disturbance over the eastern Gulf on Wednesday is expected to 
track westward along the northern Gulf Coast Thursday and Friday, 
and be very close to Lake Pontchartrain at that point, before 
weakening or dissipating. The remnants of former Tropical Storm 
Dolly are expected to enter the far southeastern Gulf by Friday, 
with disagreement on what happens beyond that point. 

Not seeing any indications of significant drying or subsidence in at 
least the global operational runs through next weekend, so we'll be 
carrying precipitation in the forecast each day. Not a lot of 
variance between the global temperature guidance, so no real targets 
of opportunity to make adjustments from the NBM.

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Thursday night)
Issued at 1050 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Very compact tropical system at roughly 215 miles due south of New
Orleans this morning. These type of systems can develop rapidly
due to their small size so its possible that it can deepen enough
to bring it to cyclone status later today since all variables are
hospitable for its development. The system has no immediate 
impacts expected inland on this side of the state but as it moves 
WNW, it will eventually have impacts for the west side. Marine 
areas will be the only real impacts locally and most if not all of
that will be well offshore. The system will provide a continued 
weakness over the area with onshore flow keeping precip numbers 
elevated today and this higher coverage should remain through much
of this week as a deep layered tropical flow should continue. The
majority of this week will be a rather diurnal pattern playing 
out with daytime storms and not a lot of activity overnight inland
and a temporal opposite of that for marine areas. The next two 
systems that would highten rain/storm chances are still embedded 
in this deep easterly flow and timing of those are still intact. 
These can easily be seen in any sat imagery with the first being 
just east of the Florida east coast and the second at around 28N 
72W. The second one is the most questionable at this time and is 
stationary at the moment. Models want to bring it closer to the 
east coast of Florida by Tue then slow it to a stall as it feels 
the east coast trough. Then what occur with the remnants of Dolly,
does it assimilate with this disturbance or does it remain 
seperate? The answers to these will eventually be solved, but for 
now, they are valid questions. The area off the east coast of 
Florida becomes quite conducive for development over the coming 
days. So, to see something eventually develop over that area would
not be surprising.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Thursday night through Sunday) 
Issued at 1050 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

The overall thinking in the extended portion of the forecast 
hasn't changed much with an active setup through the week. 
However, noticed some indications last night and there is 
definitely a trend in the medium range guidance and associated 
ensemble means towards the pattern changing as we move into next 
weekend. This shift is towards a more typical late summer setup 
with the ridge building and more centered of the plains. Thus a 
drier and warmer forecast especially late next weekend and heading
into the first full week of September. With much of the forecast 
focused on the current system just south of our coast and another 
possible tropical wave moving in around the middle part of the 
week along with a lower confidence forecast for Friday and through
next weekend we will stick with the latest NBM. This still has 
above normal PoPs for much of the area both Friday and Saturday 
but then we see PoPs start to drop. 

The main key in the extended forecast is the evolution of the mid 
lvl ridge. B late Thursday The ridge will be dominating much of the 
Mid MS Valley across the southern Appalachians while the ridge axis 
stretches from northwestern/north-central Mexico across the TN 
Valley and into the Atlantic off of the Carolina coast. Then 
beginning overnight Thursday and especially Friday the ridge begins 
to strengthen to our northwest while still wrapping back around over 
the southeastern CONUS. This could be a little worrisome as we could 
see our next tropical wave, which is expected to move into the 
north-central and northwestern Gulf mid week, possibly get trapped 
under/blocked by the ridge somewhere over eastern TX and western LA. 
If and where that occurs it could become a potential heavy rain 
producer for the back half of the week. And this heavy rain could

criteria.

interruptions could be fairly brief.

depths. Otherwise rain-free weather is in store across the area
through at least Saturday afternoon with highs in the upper 70s
to lower 80s and comfortable humidity.

allow for sufficient radiational cooling for shallow patchy fog 
development, particularly along river valleys and typical fog 
prone low spots outside of Chicago.

toward upper ridging building across the central CONUS with 
multiple waves expected to traverse the Northern Plains and 
Upper Midwest this weekend through much of the upcoming week.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 200 AM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

Surface high pressure that has made for pleasant conditions the
past couple of days is slowly departing to the east. An upper
level ridge is expected to slowly slide eastward and expand 
across the Great Plains today. There is a fairly stout MCS in
eastern South Dakota, on the east side of the ridge axis that is
slowly moving into southwestern Minnesota currently. The 
northwest flow from the ridge that is presently overhead would 
normally steer this system directly to Chicago; however, models 
are suggesting a mid level wave to pass over the northern Plains
which will help flatten the ridge. This will effectively help 
keep most of the better forcing to the north of the Wisconsin 
stateline. Regional radar trends will be monitored through the 
course of the day to ensure that no southern deviation occurs, 
but there is one other fly in the ointment which will help
prevent concerns with rain/storm chances today: surface layer 
dry air. Event the most aggressive models that have the system 
making a southern shift and entering northern Illinois run into 
issues with the dry air that is currently over the region and
shows the complex eroding away. For now, PoPs were constructed 
limiting the chances to north of Interstate 88 this afternoon 
into the early evening. There are certainly chances for 
sprinkles as south of Interstate 80, but confidence is low that 
they can make it to the surface through the dry air. With the 
better forcing to the north, thunder is not currently forecasted
for this afternoon/evening time frame.

A slightly better short wave is expected to ride over top of 
the ridge tomorrow night and Sunday morning. Forcing with this
wave will be slightly better over northern Illinois to provide 
better confidence to increase PoPs (relative to Saturday 
afternoon). Lapse rates look fairly poor leaving only narrow, 
skinny CAPE depicted in model soundings. Thunder mention was 
added to the forecast, but limited the probability to less than
25 percent as coverage is expected to be more isolated.

The previously mentioned upper level ridge will be responsible
for the weather for much of the week next week as it sits over 
much of the CONUS. There is uncertainty in the exact placement 
of the ridge, (more flat/southerly located = more 
showers/storms; more amplified/centrally located = drier) to 
merit confidence in timing and coverage through early next 
week. No major changes deviated from the chance PoPs the NBM
provided. While periods of showers and storms will be possible,
the expectation is for far more drier times that wet.

Southwest flow will help advect warmer 850 mb temperatures 
under the ridge through the week. Heat and humidity is expected 
to slowly rise through week. Models have been consistently 
showing highest heat index values (in the mid to upper 90s) by 
the middle of the week. The GFS is notably warmer than the than 
the Euro, so there is still some uncertainty on the exact heat 
values, but there is gaining confidence in another hot stretch 
of temperatures as we enter September.

At the end of the forecast time period, models are trying to 
suggest that the ridge starts to break down and returns 
northern Illinois to northwest flow overhead (which would aid
shower/storm development). The NBM is clearly picking up on 
this signal with higher end chance PoPs into next weekend. 
Timing at this distance is very fuzzy logic, but there may be 
better chances for rain/storms late Friday or Saturday.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 222 AM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

As a low level jet (LLJ) increases this morning, as sampled 
around 40 knots just 2000 ft AGL on the KLOT VAD, it is no 
surprise that shower coverage is gradually expanding over 
northern Illinois. PoPs were increased to around 30 to 40 
percent chance to match the coverage being observed. This 
southwest to northeast oriented LLJ is expected to pivot and
become slightly more easterly oriented through the morning and 
be the driving force behind an increase in shower coverage. 
There is modest effective shear present, but CAPE values and 
lapse rates are not providing confidence in overall coverage of 
thunder. That being said, there have already been small clusters
of embedded thunderstorms develop early this morning. Most 
thunder is expected to be isolated, but there could be an uptick
in thunder coverage right around and after daybreak. Current 
guidance is suggesting the LLJ will gradually diminish around 
midday allowing the showers to eventually erode and sink
southward as it falls apart. 

An upper level ridge, the center of which is currently analyzed
over Oklahoma and Texas, keeps northern Illinois and northwest 
Indiana along its northern periphery through midweek. There 
will be plenty of dry times, but as embedded waves moves through
the pattern, there will be additional periods of showers and 
storms. For example, RAP analysis is currently showing an upper 
level short wave from Rapid City, SD to around Dodge City, KS 
just behind ongoing storms in the Great Plains. There is an 
additional short wave in western Wyoming and Colorado. Models 
are suggesting that that both these waves are expected to ride 
along the top of the ridge and provide additional chances for 
precipitation overnight tonight (the Plains wave) and again 
overnight into Tuesday morning. If the ridge were to strengthen,
it could force these waves (and subsequent shower/storm 
chances) farther north. Whether or not they maintain their 
current trajectory or strength remains to be seen. For now, 
chances for showers and storms remain in the forecast through 
the middle of the week.

As the ridge remains over the CONUS through midweek, so does 
southwesterly flow at the mid-levels. This wind direction will 
aid in advecting in a warmer air mass to the western Great Lakes 
with projected 850 mb temperatures over 20C, potentially pushing
25C. Winds at the surface will also remain out of the south, 
gradually increasing dew points through the week back into the 
70s. Hotter temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s are 
expected. This combination of hot temperatures and humid 
conditions are expected to increase heat indices into the mid to
upper 90s by midweek, with the southwestern portion of the 
forecast area with a chance of exceeding 100. Chances for 
shower/storms through the weak lowers confidence in specific 
temperatures values; therefore, there was no consideration at 
this time for any heat hazard products (advisory/watch).

Models are suggesting that the ridge could break down by the end
of the work week. That will help the hottest of temperatures to
cool off a bit, but it will return the upper level flow pattern 
to the northwest and thus bring with it additional chances for 
showers/storms over the weekend.

DK

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 231 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

A shortwave disturbance over northeastern Iowa will continue to
drive showers and embedded thunderstorms eastward through early
this evening, with the greatest coverage expected north of 
I-80. While a 20% chance for lightning remains, poor mid-level 
lapse rates across northern Illinois should limit thunderstorms 
to isolated coverage.

Following the eastward departure of this short-wave impulse 
this evening, a southwesterly low-level jet will ramp up again 
overnight, with the core expected to reside over IA 
northeastward into southern WI. Associated isentropic upglide 
(warm air advection) may thus foster more isolated to scattered 
showers and thunderstorms late tonight into early Monday 
morning. Thereafter, capping is likely to curtail the threat of 
convection for much of the area into Monday afternoon. However, 
another short-wave impulse is progged to translate eastward 
towards northwestern IL late in the day, and thus may act as the
impetus for isolated to widely scattered afternoon development 
across northwestern IL after 2 pm. Should this activity occur, 
~40 kt of mid-level westerly flow could support a few stronger 
storms across northwestern IL late in the afternoon. Confidence 
remains low with the extent of this threat. 

Convective trends continue to be of low confidence Monday night
into Tuesday morning. Nevertheless, low (20-30%)chances for 
storms continue due to the persistent warm-air advection pattern
in combination with additional smaller scale perturbations 
likely to transition eastward across southern WI through the 
mid-level ridge axis. The better focus for storms may remain in 
southern WI, but at this time, cannot rule out storms as far 
south as the I-80 corridor. The SPC day 3 severe outlook (for 
Tuesday) places most areas north of I-80 in a level 1 of 5 
threat. So, while confidence in the coverage of storms remains 
low into Tuesday morning, the meteorological environment will be
supportive of a conditional threat for strong storms. 

Outside of the threat of storms through Tuesday morning, 
temperatures and humidity levels will be on the rise through 
mid-week as the airmass under the expansive mid/upper-level 
ridge continues to warm. We anticipate high temperatures in the 
upper 80s Monday, the low 90s Tuesday and the low to mid 90s 
Wednesday. In spite of us being past the peak timing for 
evapotranspiration, limited mixing under an inversion centered 
near 850 mb should keep dew points in the low to mid 70s during 
peak heating, particularly on Tuesday and Wednesday, resulting 
in peak heat indices in the 100 to 105 range. 

Relief from the heat looks plausible later in the week as a
backdoor cold front sags southward into the area. However, this
looks to come at the expense of a period of more active weather
(a period or two of thunderstorms, some possibly strong) at the
end of the week. The specifics such as the timing of the front
and best potential for thunderstorms remain a bit unclear at
this point, but storm chances begin to ramp up across our area
late Wednesday night into Thursday.

KJB

A shortwave disturbance over northeastern Iowa will continue to
drive showers and embedded thunderstorms eastward through early
this evening, with the greatest coverage expected north of 
I-80. While a 20% chance for lightning remains, poor mid-level 
lapse rates across northern Illinois should limit thunderstorms 
to isolated coverage.

Following the eastward departure of this short-wave impulse 
this evening, a southwesterly low-level jet will ramp up again 
overnight, with the core expected to reside over IA 
northeastward into southern WI. Associated isentropic upglide 
(warm air advection) may thus foster more isolated to scattered 
showers and thunderstorms late tonight into early Monday 
morning. Thereafter, capping is likely to curtail the threat of 
convection for much of the area into Monday afternoon. However, 
another short-wave impulse is progged to translate eastward 
towards northwestern IL late in the day, and thus may act as the
impetus for isolated to widely scattered afternoon development 
across northwestern IL after 2 pm. Should this activity occur, 
~40 kt of mid-level westerly flow could support a few stronger 
storms across northwestern IL late in the afternoon. Confidence 
remains low with the extent of this threat. 

Convective trends continue to be of low confidence Monday night
into Tuesday morning. Nevertheless, low (20-30%)chances for 
storms continue due to the persistent warm-air advection pattern
in combination with additional smaller scale perturbations 
likely to transition eastward across southern WI through the 
mid-level ridge axis. The better focus for storms may remain in 
southern WI, but at this time, cannot rule out storms as far 
south as the I-80 corridor. The SPC day 3 severe outlook (for 
Tuesday) places most areas north of I-80 in a level 1 of 5 
threat. So, while confidence in the coverage of storms remains 
low into Tuesday morning, the meteorological environment will be
supportive of a conditional threat for strong storms. 

Outside of the threat of storms through Tuesday morning, 
temperatures and humidity levels will be on the rise through 
mid-week as the airmass under the expansive mid/upper-level 
ridge continues to warm. We anticipate high temperatures in the 
upper 80s Monday, the low 90s Tuesday and the low to mid 90s 
Wednesday. In spite of us being past the peak timing for 
evapotranspiration, limited mixing under an inversion centered 
near 850 mb should keep dew points in the low to mid 70s during 
peak heating, particularly on Tuesday and Wednesday, resulting 
in peak heat indices in the 100 to 105 range.

backdoor cold front sags southward into the area. However, this
looks to come at the expense of a period of more active weather
(a period or two of thunderstorms, some possibly strong) at the
end of the week. The specifics such as the timing of the front
and best potential for thunderstorms remain a bit unclear at
this point, but storm chances begin to ramp up across our area
late Wednesday night into Thursday.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 200 AM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Thunderstorms have fizzled out, but isolated showers fester over
the forecast area early this morning. Similar to last night, a
southwest to northeast low level jet (LLJ) is expected to
amplify prior to daybreak and help induce additional shower and
storm coverage. There is lower confidence on the exact 
coverage; but considering how impressive last night/yesterday 
morning's coverage ended up being, widely scattered showers and 
storms can be expected through daybreak before gradually 
diminishing (as the LLJ weakens) and moves east. Forcing becomes
fairly nebulous behind the LLJ. Most areas should receive a 
period of dry conditions around midday, but maintained slight 
chance PoPs for a stray diurnal shower that might pop-up this 
afternoon, mainly north of Interstate 88.

Stepping back and zooming out for a second, GOES IR and water 
vapor satellite imagery currently shows broad cloud cover 
sweeping across the CONUS from the Four Corners, to the 
Minnesota arrowhead, down to our nation's capital. Their 
movement is riding over an upper level ridge that has dominated 
the forecast for the last several days. IR is showing showers 
and storms over eastern Colorado/northwestern Kansas that is 
collocated with an upper level short wave embedded in the 
ridge. This wave is expected to quickly move across the Great 
Plains and head toward southwestern Wisconsin today. Model 
soundings are showing a fairly strong cap and a robust dry air 
over much of the area this afternoon and early evening with 
DCAPE values around 1000 J/kg in northwest Illinois. The cap 
might be enough to inhibit shower and storm development, but 
lapse rates are expected to steepen along with modest deep layer
shear with the arrival of the short wave. Any elevated storm 
that develops upstream strengthen and possibly produce some 
hail up to the size of a quarter or potentially localized 
damaging wind gusts, mainly for areas north of Interstate 88. 
The main bit of uncertainty is the exact track of the wave. If 
it follows the ridge, it could move right over northern 
Illinois, with favored areas closer to the Wisconsin stateline. 
But some models have a slightly more northern track into 
Wisconsin which would limit shower/storm coverage.

Even as the wave passes to the northeast, broad warm air
advection behind the wave could allow for festering showers once
again overnight into early Tuesday morning. For now, kept 
"silent" PoPs (10 to 14 percent chance) with no formal forecast 
mention, but trends will be monitored. At the risk of sounding 
like a broken record, but models are suggesting yet another 
wave embedded within the ridge is expected to pass nearby on 
Tuesday morning/early afternoon. However, models are showing a 
lot of disagreement with this wave. The NAM currently has the 
northernmost solution that may keep most of the forecast area 
dry, whereas the latest 00Z guidance is starting to bring that 
wave closer down into northern Illinois. With increasing 
instability ahead of the wave, it provides another chance where 
storms could become strong to severe. This also just highlights 
the pattern that the region currently finds itself in with 
persistent waves within the ridge pattern that keeps periodic 
shower/storm chances in the forecast. However, shower/storm 
chances on Tuesday could impact the temperature forecast.

As the upper level ridge slowly ambles east through midweek,
southwest winds are expected to advect in a warmer air mass and
higher dewpoints into the region. High temperatures are expected
to climb into the low 90s with dew point temperatures into the
low to possibly mid 70s. Models have been fairly consistent in
suggesting Wednesday could be the hottest day of the week where
heat index values could reach the mid to upper 90s for much of
the forecast area, and better chances that they could meet or 
exceed 100 south of Interstate 80. Confidence lowers in exact
heat values from south to north across the forecast area with
greatest uncertainty closer to the top of the ridge (north of
Interstate 80) given the better chances for showers and storms
there.

Models are suggesting that the ridge could break down by the 
end of the work week. That will help the hottest of temperatures
cool off a bit, but it will return the upper level flow pattern
to the northwest and thus bring with it additional chances for 
showers/storms toward and over the weekend.

DK

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 247 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

While we're about to turn the page on the calendar to 
meteorological fall, the weather pattern is much more 
reminiscent of mid-summer with a strong mid-upper level ridge of
high pressure from the central plains east to the mid-Atlantic.
Low amplitude shortwave troughs continue to ride along the 
flanks of this upper ridge, with one such wave responsible for 
the elevated showers and t-storms over northern Illinois this 
afternoon. Short range guidance has largely been performing 
poorly handling these small scale features and their associated 
convection, so the short term forecast was driven largely by 
extrapolating the shortwave eastward using water vapor imagery. 
The trough axis and associated forcing should be moving east to 
Lake Michigan early this evening, so would anticipate a decrease
in coverage of precip late this afternoon into early this 
evening from west to east. 

The next shortwave trough of interest is located over the 4 
corners region and should turn northeast and east around the 
western periphery of the ridge tonight into Tuesday. Guidance 
that has initialized this wave generally tracks it north of our 
CWA Tuesday afternoon as the upper ridge strengthens a bit over 
the mid-Mississippi Valley. An axis of very strong instability 
with minimal convective inhibition is expected from Iowa east 
into southern Wisconsin and far northern Illinois. CAM guidance,
which hasn't performed well lately, keeps convection with this 
feature focused mostly north of the IL/WI border. Despite what 
looks to be only a glancing shot of forcing with this shortwave,
we have opted to carry chance PoPs tomorrow afternoon near the 
WI border and Slight chace PoPs south to nearly I-80. If any 
mature convection can become established in this environment 
Tuesday afternoon, severe thunderstorms would be likely given 
the very strong instability and 30-40 kt of 0-6 km shear. 
Confidence remains low given the potential for the stronger 
forcing to remain north of the uncapped/strongly unstable air 
mass over our region. If it becomes clear that forcing will be 
sufficient for storms into our CWA (most likely northern CWA), 
then a substantially greater risk of severe thunderstorms would 
be likely.

The other big story is the late season heat and humidity. 
Pretty good agreement among the various models that 925 mb temps
in the mid to upper 20s Celsius will advect into the area 
Tuesday and Wednesday. This should support high temperatures in 
the lower to potentially mid 90s both afternoons, though the 
potential for convection/convective debris cloudiness leads to 
lower confidence in temperatures north of I-80. 

In addition to the heat, very humid conditions are expected 
with 70 degree dewpoints pooling from Iowa east across northern 
and central Illinois into Indiana. While we are past peak 
evapotranspiration (ET) season, climatologically ET in early 
September is not negligible and tends to be similar to what we 
typically see in mid-late June. Evidence of this ET was quite 
apparent today with dewpoints jumping 4-8F late this morning 
into early this afternoon from southern IA east into 
northern/central IL. Morning soundings suggest this jump in 
surface dewpoints wasn't the result of mixing down high moisture
and with lower dewpoints upstream, this jump wasn't from 
horizontal advection, strongly suggesting it was largely driven 
by ET. There is reason to be concerned that this ET could result
in dewpoints locally reaching the mid to even locally upper 70s
Tuesday/Wednesday afternoons, especially in the more heavily 
agricultural areas. 

The combination of high temperatures in the low to potentially mid 
90s and dewpoints in the 70s should result in peak afternoon heat

flanks of this upper ridge, with one such wave responsible for 
the elevated showers and t-storms over northern Illinois this 
afternoon. Short range guidance has largely been performing 
poorly handling these small scale features and their associated 
convection, so the short term forecast was driven largely by 
extrapolating the shortwave eastward using water vapor imagery. 
The trough axis and associated forcing should be moving east to 
Lake Michigan early this evening, so would anticipate a decrease
in coverage of precip late this afternoon into early this 
evening from west to east. 

The next shortwave trough of interest is located over the 4 
corners region and should turn northeast and east around the 
western periphery of the ridge tonight into Tuesday. Guidance 
that has initialized this wave generally tracks it north of our 
CWA Tuesday afternoon as the upper ridge strengthens a bit over 
the mid-Mississippi Valley. An axis of very strong instability 
with minimal convective inhibition is expected from Iowa east 
into southern Wisconsin and far northern Illinois. CAM guidance,
which hasn't performed well lately, keeps convection with this 
feature focused mostly north of the IL/WI border. Despite what 
looks to be only a glancing shot of forcing with this shortwave,

mature convection can become established in this environment

agricultural areas.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 152 AM CDT Tue Sep 1 2026

Though Tonight...

Early morning GOES-19 water vapor imagery depicts an expansive 
summer-like heat dome centered over the middle Mississippi River
Valley with RAP-analyzed 500mb heights near 5960m over Paducah,
Kentucky. Meanwhile, an upper-level low was centered near the 
Manitoba and Ontario borders in southern Canada. Quasi-zonal 
flow stretches between the upper-level low to the north and heat
dome to the south from the Black Hills region eastward through 
the Lower Great Lakes. Closer to the surface, an expansive 
region of unseasonably moist low-level air characterized by dew 
points in the low to mid 70s encompasses much of the Great 
Lakes, Upper Mississippi River, and middle Mississippi River 
valleys. The large-scale pattern is more typical of the middle 
of July than the first day of September. 

The primary concern today are dangerous heat. Owing to the very
wet summer (90 day observed precipitation departures were 200 
to 300% of normal across parts of Illinois and Indiana), 
agricultural evapotranspiration is still in full swing. Dew 
points yesterday climbed into the mid to upper 70s across much 
of the forecast area, and frankly there are no reasons why the 
same won't happen today. With 850mb temperatures peaking in the 
+22 to +23 range today and tomorrow, dry bulb high temperatures 
should have no problem reaching the low to mid 90s. When 
combined with dew points in the mid to upper 70s, widespread 
heat index values of 105 to locally 110F (wet bulb globe 
temperatures of 87 to 90F) appear to be a good bet today. 

The only fly in the ointment is the low probability threat for 
thunderstorms and associated free air conditioning (whether by 
cloud cover or precipitation). Early this morning, have been 
keeping a close eye on an elongated west-to-east band of ACCAS 
extending from near Omaha, Nebraska to Davenport, Iowa. Per the 
00Z RAOBs from OAX and DVN, the ACCAS field is rooted at the 
base of an EML plume in which lapse rates range from 7.5 to 8 
K/km from 850 to 500 mb. Over the past hour or two, the ACCAS 
field has gotten increasingly agitated east of Omaha, presumably
owing to increasing low-level confluence on the nose of a 
modest but nevertheless intensifying 850mb low-level jet and at 
least a glancing blow of upper-level diffluence in the right 
entrance region of a jet streak propagating into the Great 
Lakes.

In the absence of more pronounced forcing for ascent, it seems 
like the most likely scenario is for thunderstorms to struggle 
to develop and maintain themselves across Iowa early this 
morning. However, should they develop and become established, 
they will have access to a highway of moisture-laden instability
(MUCAPE >3000 J/kg) that points directly to Chicago. When also 
considering access to 30 to 35kt of westerly upper-level flow on
the southern edge of the aforementioned jet streak, any 
established storm would be prone to developing into an eastward-
racing cluster with a threat for damaging winds (again, 
sweeping across much of our area). Timing would be from mid-
morning to early afternoon (call it 9 AM to 3 PM from west to
east). At this point, the chance of this outcome seems low 
(call it a 10 to 20% probability), but will continue to watch 
trends across Iowa this morning in case the odds start to turn. 

Will also note there is a threat for thunderstorms to develop 
at any point this afternoon when instability is maximized, 
though am currently not seeing really any mechanisms to force 
ascent beyond the window from this morning within the neutral 
mid-level height-tendency regime. 

With the more likely scenario appearing to be being no storms 
today, will go ahead and expand the Heat Advisory to now 
encompass the entire area. While the Heat Advisory will expire 
at 9 PM, tonight will still be balmy with overnight lows in the 
low to mid 70s. 


Wednesday...

On Wednesday, ensemble guidance is in fair agreement that an 
upper-level shortwave embedded in the upper-level anticyclonic 
flow around the ridge will propagate into the Upper Mississippi 
River Valley and upper Great Lakes. Depending on the evolution 
of thunderstorms tonight in the northern Plains, can easily 
envision an MCS or two riding across Minnesota, central 
Wisconsin, and Lower Michigan on Wednesday. With all forcing 
remaining well north of our area, the chance for storms on 
Wednesday will be even lower than today. 

Interestingly, guidance suggests dew points may be a touch 
lower on Wednesday compared to today which would lead to heat 
index values more in the range of 100 to 105 versus 105 to
110F. However, will continue to lean on evapotranspiration 
being a big factor and forecast another day with dangerous 
heat.

With a subtle signal in guidance for outflow originating in 
Wisconsin to creep southward into northern Illinois, am not 
quite ready to expand the inherited Heat Advisory for Wednesday 
that currently encompasses areas south of Interstate 80 to 
instead cover the entire area. Regardless, Wednesday looks like 
another hot and humid day. 


Thursday and Friday...

The upper-level ridge will finally start to break down Thursday
and Friday, placing our area within reach of upper-level 
shortwaves propagating along the northern periphery of the heat 
dome. As a result, Thursday and Friday will carry a threat for 
severe thunderstorms in the general region (the tail end of the 
00Z RRFS is quite a look for our area). Depending on eventual 
convective footprints, areas south of I-80 may still be baking 
in the heat one or both days possibly requiring an extension of 
the Heat Advisory. We'll be able to sort out those details when 
we get closer. 


Saturday onward...

Ensemble model guidance favors a surface high pressure system 
dropping southward into the Great Lakes region this weekend 
finally breaking the hot and humid pattern. With that said, 
quasi-northwest flow may develop by early next week bringing a 
return of showers and thunderstorms to the general region.
