A large heat dome remains stalled over the Lower Mississippi 
River Valley south of a slow-moving upper-level low currently in
central Ontario. Quasi-zonal flow remains in place between both
features and atop a stationary front across the central Great 
Lakes. A short-wavelength upper-level trough embedded in the 
zonal flow is currently supporting several clusters of showers 
and storms along the stationary front stretching from 
northwestern Iowa through central Wisconsin. Meanwhile, south of
the front and indeed across our area, it is a warm and muggy 
night with current air temperatures in the mid to upper 70s (dew
points in the low to mid 70s). 

Based on the continued east-northeasterly trajectory of the 
aforementioned shortwave, current expectations are that all 
clusters of showers and storms along the stationary front will 
remain north of our area through the morning hours. Even if any 
outflow makes it to northern Illinois this morning, it should 
be shallow enough to erode fairly quickly. So barring any 
unexpected southward jogs in the thunderstorm clusters or 
stronger southward outflow pushes, today is setting up to be 
another hot and humid day. Compared to yesterday, mixing 
profiles today look a hair deeper which may modestly offset 
evapotranspirational enhancement to dew points. Regardless, will
continue to lean on NAM/HRDPS guidance which shows dew points 
rebounding to the mid to locally upper 70s today. When paired 
with highs in the lower 90s, heat index values should approach 
105F again. For this reason, did expand the inherited Heat 
Advisory to encompass the entire area. If mixing is more 
effective today, suppose a stray shower or storm may attempt to 
develop this afternoon though coverage should be isolated at 
best. 

Tonight, the stationary front will begin a southward sag toward
the Illinois and Wisconsin state line. Broad and largely 
unfocused low- level flow atop the front may encourage the 
development of a shower or thunderstorm near the frontal 
boundary at any time (not unlike what we saw the past few 
nights), so will carry low-end (20%) PoPs north of I-88 through 
daybreak. Otherwise, tonight is setting up to be a repeat of 
early this morning with seasonably warm overnight lows and 
continued muggy conditions. 

Forecast confidence lowers Thursday and Thursday night. 
Deterministic guidance suggests an upper-level shortwave will 
round the ridge toward the Iowa/Wisconsin/northern Illinois 
vicinity toward daybreak accompanied by an uptick in coverage of
showers and storms. Provided this occurs, at least some 
footprint of cloud cover and cooler temperatures would be 
expected across our area lasting into early afternoon. 
Thereafter, guidance is hinting at another upper-level wave 
approaching the Great Lakes by early afternoon which may lead to
another round of storms in the general region lasting through 
the early morning hours of Friday. If convective coverage is 
minimized in the morning, the afternoon round could end up 
fairly problematic with a reservoir of moisture-laden 
instability and increasing deep- layer shear to support all 
modes of severe thunderstorms (including a threat for flash 
flooding). However if the footprint of morning showers and 
storms is vast, could also envision evolution of thunderstorms 
Thursday afternoon being pretty messy with a lower ceiling for 
intensity. At this point, see too many conditionalities to offer
more than broad-brushed chance (20 to 40%) PoPs. Will also hold
off on issuing any new Heat Advisory for parts of the area 
Thursday in favor of evaluating future model trends in potential
convective coverage. 

Friday into Saturday, ensemble guidance suggests the upper- 
level ridge will retrograde westward placing the Great Lakes 
into the precarious upper-level northwest flow regime. With the 
reservoir of moisture-laden instability remaining in place 
across the Great Lakes region, can easily envision several more 
rounds of (severe) storms in the general region through Saturday
night. At least a brief break in the pattern (both with respect
to humidity levels and temperatures) is anticipated early next 
week.

***UPDATE***

The threat of showers and thunderstorms this morning has stayed to
the north and west of our four counties so far this morning. We
are watching an enhancement just off the coast that could clip 
San Luis Obispo County in the next few hours. For the afternoon
hours, with plenty of sunshine and a still tropical airmass, the
risks will transition to the more traditional mountain and deserts
areas. None of the high-res models show anything forming over our
mountains, likely due to the lack of any upper level disturbances
to kick it off, but all the other ingredients are there to at
least maintain a low risk. If any thunderstorms form, the impacts
will be more gusty winds and fire starts, with less concern for
heavy rain and flooding. 

On the temperature side of the house, it was still very warm last
night thanks to this tropical airmass, but less warm than the
previous night thanks to less cloud cover. At 9am, the temperature
trends have flipped from 5 degrees below 24 hours ago to 5-10
degrees above thanks to the far more abundant sunshine. Expecting
this trend to continue and increase, with a hot and muggy day on 
tap. The current suite of Heat Warnings and Advisories will remain
in play as a result.

The big decision for today will be what to do with tomorrow.
Temperatures and moisture will be down from today. It will be a
big drop for San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Counties. For Los
Angeles and Ventura Counties, that drop will only be a little, 
with the big drop on track for Sunday. As such, will be 
considering Heat Advisories to cover the period from after the 
current warnings expire to the end of the day on Saturday. The 
area most likely to see these advisories are the valleys and 
inland coastal areas, but will flesh that out in the next hour or 
two.

still linger offshore. While elevated convection dropped off
overnight over land, thunderstorms were still firing off near

chances for any storms or light showers today will be north of Pt
Conception. And even though cloud coverage south of there is 
starting to decrease, PW's are still over 1.5" locally so the 
muggy-ness will continue at least one more day. And in fact, 
temperatures in most areas south of Pt Conception should rebound 
back to very similar temperatures as Wednesday with weak onshore 
flow and more sunshine. Helping that cause will be the very warm

far enough to the north to not be concern with any rain or strong
winds, but it will maintain below normal temperatures. To clarify
however, with this being the hottest time of the year, below 
normal temperatures does not mean it is time to dust off the
jackets. It will still feel warm, but thankfully not hot like it 
was last week. Tropical moisture will stay away from the region as
well so it will also not feel as muggy as it did last week. With 
ocean temperatures still in the 70s however, it will still feel 
more humid than usual.

as well, and should deepen a little more tomorrow as the trough
sags to the south. Would expect a spot or two to see drizzle in 
the morning where the clouds develop, especially near the Central
Coast foothills. Solid night through morning low clouds are most 
likely on the Central Coast, but coverage to the south should 
remain spotty thanks to the warmer ocean temperatures, despite the
marine layer being just as deep. It is impossible to predict
exactly where those random spots of clouds will form. 

Sundowner winds will continue each night over southwest Santa
Barbara County and flirt with an Advisory each time. Tonight looks
just under Advisory levels, while Tuesday and Wednesday night 
look just over.

.LONG TERM (FRI-MON)...31/140 PM.

Little change expected on Friday compared to the first half of the
week.

All eyes remain focused on the Labor Day holiday weekend period. A
Hurricane is likely to develop by Wednesday or Thursday from the 
clump of clouds currently just off the Baja coast. Once it forms,
it will likely move to the northwest through Saturday and towards
southern California. The big question is where will it head after
Saturday. Some deterministic models, like the current GFS, keeps 
the storm moving northward and right through southern California 
by Monday or Tuesday. Others, like the deterministic ECMWF, show 
the storm turning to the west and never even sniffing California. 
These are just two of many projections, but they do represent the
two extreme scenarios between a major rain and wind event and 
little to nothing. Peering into the ensemble solutions, they 
suggest that the heavy rain scenario is the least likely outcome 
(5-10% of the 100 projections have 2+ inches of rain). The 
completely dry scenario comprises 20-30% of the solutions. Which 
means in terms of rain, the most likely outcome is for some light
rain impacting the holiday weekend. The wind story is similar, 
with a low but non-zero chance of strong east winds causing fire 
and downed tree concerns. With all that said, this is definitely a
period to monitor with a range of outcomes on the table. Due to
the rarity of this storm, expecting there to be a lot of
uncertainty even as we get to the weekend, but hopefully some 
details will come more into focus by mid-week once the storm 
actually form. 

There is growing confidence for significant impacts at the coast
however. Unless the storm takes a full left turn after Saturday,
the south swell will be pumping through Tuesday, especially
considering the swells from the current Hurricane Karina also
still around. The evening high tides are also expected to be near
7 feet by Monday. The most likely scenario would result in high 
surf during a busy holiday weekend and moderate coastal flooding 
on south facing beaches. If the storm gets closer to the coast, 
those impacts will be amplified.

.SHORT TERM...
(Rest of today through Wednesday)
Issued at 120 PM EDT Tue Sep 1 2026

Upper-air analyses today have confirmed the presence of a TUTT-like 
feature to north of the Bahamas, which has directly resulted in 
anomalously moist conditions across South Florida. Both ACARS 
soundings and mesoanalysis data have shown regional PWATs between 
the 2.1-2.4" range early this afternoon, which is precisely between 
the 90-97th climatological percentiles for the date based off the
ECMWF EFI ensemble forecast and between 1-2" inches above average
based on the NAEFS standardized anomaly. Marine DMAX has allowed 
the bulk of the shower and thunderstorm activity to stay mostly 
offshore this morning, but diurnal heating and this highly-
saturated atmosphere will imminently result in the development of 
widely scattered showers and thunderstorms across our region 
through early this evening. High-res models indicate the highest 
coverage of convection occurring over the interior and SW Florida 
where both our local sea breezes are forecast to converge.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 219 AM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Today and Tonight... Today's weather will be driven by warm air
advection. First and most obvious warm and moist air is moving 
in brining us higher temperatures and dew points. This will 
bring heat index values into the 90s with the higher values 
south (southern MN/west central WI) and lower north (central 
MN/northwest WI). This warm air advection will also occur along 
a warm front and the lift from this front will provide some 
chances for storm development. The challenge for CI will be 
overcoming the cap we have in place this morning. So far this 
cap has held and no development has been noted. For anything 
that does occur this morning CI will need to occur over the 
Dakotas and survive into Minnesota. We do have strong elevated 
instability, so elevated storms could maintain themselves if 
they have a deep enough updraft. This afternoon and evening 
daytime heating should help to break this cap, but the front 
will lift north such that chances will be mainly in central and 
northern Minnesota. The main severe chance will be tied more to 
the cold front moving across the Dakotas. So severe will be tied
to storms that initiate to the west and track into Minnesota 
overnight. How linear this storms go will play a big part in
determining the risk type. More linear being more wind and more
discrete favoring hail. SPC has also noted a low tornado chance
tied to the area along the warm front.

Monday and Tuesday... The cold front will pass through Minnesota on
Monday providing some relief from the moisture. This will keep
the higher dew points and therefore the heat index values above
90 in western Wisconsin. With clearer skies temperatures won't
be much cooler, if at all, in Minnesota but the lower dew points
will be noticeable. These lower dew points should spread into
Wisconsin on Tuesday expanding the relief.

Tuesday night into Wednesday... Another shortwave trough moving
across the plains will provide our next chance for rain Tuesday
night into Wednesday. Thankfully this looks more like what we
saw on Saturday morning with a more widespread light rain rather
than the more isolated nature of what is forecast for today.
Looking at forecast soundings the greatest challenge will be 
low level dry air. This means it will take a while before rain 
starts to reach the surface. This will also be a limiting factor
in strong storms, as it will greatly limit instability. Looking
towards ensemble systems there is actually good agreement for 
this far out, which is why we are already seeing higher PoPs in
the NBM. Just more of a timing displacement right now with the 
GEFS/GEPS earlier than the ENS.

Rest of the Week... Ensembles get much more dispersive after
Wednesday, but continue to show activity. This remains the same
long term forecast we have had for much of the past week with a
more active and warm pattern. This keep highs in the 80s with a 
low confidence of which days will see rain until at least the 
mid range forecast (about 3 days out).

this time of year (i.e. a mean of 58 degrees for late August). So 
aside from this surface front not providing much precip today, dew 
points are expected to fall back closer to climatology levels for

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 409 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

There's an impressive bowling ball upper low over southern 
Saskatchewan and Manitoba this afternoon, which is driving a cold 
across western WI and far southeast MN. Our position south of this 
upper low puts us in its zone of subsidence and mid-level dry air, 
which means we get yet another dry cold front, which seems par for 
the course for an August that will see MSP finish the month with 
just 0.46" of rain (we average 4.34"), which is the 4th driest 
August on record and just the 8th out of 156 years where the Twin 
Cities failed to get at least 1" of rain in the month of August. 
With that said, we can't completely rule out rain in the MPX area 
this evening, but that chance is in Eau Claire and Chippewa 
counties, to the east of Chippewa Falls and Eau Claire. East of the 
cold front, it's oppressive for the last day of August, with 
temperatures in the upper 80s, dewpoints in the mid 70s, and heat 
index values in the mid 90s. All of this heat and humidity is 
translating into instability, with a pool of 3000+ j/kg of mlCAPE 
forecast develop ahead of the front. Although isolated storm chances 
look better east of the MPX area, the HRRR has been initiating 
storms in eastern Eau Claire county around 23z from the 15z run 
through its most current run (19z), so we will have to keep an eye 
on the storm potential out around Stanley and Augusta. After that, 
the rest of the night will be quiet, with drier air moving in 
limiting the fog potential in MN (where dewpoints are in the mid 50s 
across central MN). WI will still have radiational fog potential as 
they will hold on to dewpoints in the 60s through the night.

This drier airmass moving in today will stay with us through the day 
on Tuesday, with dewpoints in the upper 40s to lower 60s making 
highs Tuesday in the 80s more tolerable. 

Tuesday night is when things start to turn more active as a 
shortwave coming out of the southwest monsoon travels across 
southern MN. Most guidance shows storms developing on the nose of 
the LLJ and riding the elevated CAPE gradient east Tuesday night. 
Looking at the HREF/REFS, the pool of high muCAPE (over 3000 j/kg) 
will remain near/north of the I-80 corridor in Iowa, with the LLJ 
nosing up into northern Iowa. This all points to the MN/IA border 
being the zone most conducive to seeing thunderstorms/heavy rain, 
with a lighter overrunning precipitation area getting about as far 
north as the Twin Cities metro, which will likely mean central MN 
into northwest WI misses out on this one. Based on where the large 
scale forcing is forecast to be, the NBM this morning looked to have 
displaced it's higher PoPs/QPF a bit too far north, so did nudge 
PoPs a bit south Tuesday night to get closer to where the forcing 
is. 

Wednesday through Labor Day begins a period of high confidence in 
summer-like warmth and humidity for the first week of meteorological 
fall, but low confidence on precipitation. Figuring out severe 
weather potential comes down to figuring out where moisture (for 
said storms), forcing (something to provide large scale ascent for 
that moist air), instability (so that the ascending moist air goes 
up in a convective updraft), and wind shear (let's organize those 
storms!) all come together. The large scale weather pattern through 
the weekend will become amplified as a trough digs into the Pac NW. 
As it digs into the Pac NW, we see the ridge over the central CONUS 
amplify, with a westerly to southwest flow developing aloft locally. 
This setup will pump deep moisture into our region from the Gulf and 
southwest Monsoon. Looking at the 4 ingredients, we'll have plenty 
of moisture (mean EPS Pwats are 150% to 200% of normal through the 
weekend), given the heat and humidity, instability will be ample, 
and with the upper jet always overhead/nearby, we'll have ample wind 
shear as well. The big uncertainty through the weekend is the 
forcing variable. With the building upper ridge, forcing looks 
subtle, with precipitation chances tied to where the warm front is 
on a daily basis and where any weak waves move through in the upper 
flow. In other words, it's mesoscale features that will be driving 
our precipitations, which is hard to parse out more than 48 hours in 
advance. The result is what you get with this forecast, numerous low

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 409 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

There's an impressive bowling ball upper low over southern 
Saskatchewan and Manitoba this afternoon, which is driving a 
cold across western WI and far southeast MN. Our position south 
of this upper low puts us in its zone of subsidence and mid-
level dry air, which means we get yet another dry cold front, 
which seems par for the course for an August that will see MSP 
finish the month with just 0.46" of rain (we average 4.34"), 
which is the 4th driest August on record and just the 8th out of
156 years where the Twin Cities failed to get at least 1" of 
rain in the month of August. With that said, we can't completely
rule out rain in the MPX area this evening, but that chance is 
in Eau Claire and Chippewa counties, to the east of Chippewa 
Falls and Eau Claire. East of the cold front, it's oppressive 
for the last day of August, with temperatures in the upper 80s, 
dewpoints in the mid 70s, and heat index values in the mid 90s. 
All of this heat and humidity is translating into instability, 
with a pool of 3000+ j/kg of mlCAPE forecast develop ahead of 
the front. Although isolated storm chances look better east of 
the MPX area, the HRRR has been initiating storms in eastern Eau
Claire county around 23z from the 15z run through its most 
current run (19z), so we will have to keep an eye on the storm 
potential out around Stanley and Augusta. After that, the rest 
of the night will be quiet, with drier air moving in limiting 
the fog potential in MN (where dewpoints are in the mid 50s 
across central MN). WI will still have radiational fog potential
as they will hold on to dewpoints in the 60s through the night.

This drier airmass moving in today will stay with us through the
day on Tuesday, with dewpoints in the upper 40s to lower 60s 
making highs Tuesday in the 80s more tolerable. 

Tuesday night is when things start to turn more active as a  
shortwave coming out of the southwest monsoon travels across 
southern MN. Most guidance shows storms developing on the nose 
of the LLJ and riding the elevated CAPE gradient east Tuesday 
night. Looking at the HREF/REFS, the pool of high muCAPE (over 
3000 j/kg) will remain near/north of the I-80 corridor in Iowa, 
with the LLJ nosing up into northern Iowa. This all points to 
the MN/IA border being the zone most conducive to seeing 
thunderstorms/heavy rain, with a lighter overrunning 
precipitation area getting about as far north as the Twin Cities
metro, which will likely mean central MN into northwest WI 
misses out on this one. Based on where the large scale forcing 
is forecast to be, the NBM this morning looked to have displaced
it's higher PoPs/QPF a bit too far north, so did nudge PoPs a 
bit south Tuesday night to get closer to where the forcing is. 

Wednesday through Labor Day begins a period of high confidence
in summer-like warmth and humidity for the first week of 
meteorological fall, but low confidence on precipitation. 
Figuring out severe weather potential comes down to figuring out
where moisture (for said storms), forcing (something to provide
large scale ascent for that moist air), instability (so that 
the ascending moist air goes up in a convective updraft), and 
wind shear (let's organize those storms!) all come together. The
large scale weather pattern through the weekend will become 
amplified as a trough digs into the Pac NW. As it digs into the 
Pac NW, we see the ridge over the central CONUS amplify, with a 
westerly to southwest flow developing aloft locally. This setup 
will pump deep moisture into our region from the Gulf and 
southwest Monsoon. Looking at the 4 ingredients, we'll have 
plenty of moisture (mean EPS Pwats are 150% to 200% of normal 
through the weekend), given the heat and humidity, instability 
will be ample, and with the upper jet always overhead/nearby, 
we'll have ample wind shear as well. The big uncertainty through
the weekend is the forcing variable. With the building upper 
ridge, forcing looks subtle, with precipitation chances tied to 
where the warm front is on a daily basis and where any weak 
waves move through in the upper flow. In other words, it's 
mesoscale features that will be driving our precipitations, 
which is hard to parse out more than 48 hours in advance. The 
result is what you get with this forecast, numerous low chances 
for precipitation through the holiday weekend. At this point, 
about the best we can say is whatever we get, it looks to be 
predominately nocturnal in nature. Will we manage to finally 
cash in on a potential active weather pattern? Maybe, but when 
it comes to forecasting precipitation in a drought, I like to 
live be the maxim of when in drought, leave it out.

.DISCUSSION...

Welcome to meteorological fall! It will not feel much like fall
though with temperatures continuing to be warm (generally in the
80s) even for the peak of summer. In addition we also have a 
chance for some strong to severe thunderstorms tonight and
almost daily chances for more rain/storms. Even though next 
week is starting to look a little cooler, it will be a while 
before we get fall weather.

Today and Tonight... Another morning of ample radiative cooling
and light winds is providing for some patchy fog. Some areas 
could be locally dense, but it will not be widespread. The cold 
front has now passed through all of the area, but it won't be 
much cooler today as the warm airmass remains over us. The 
bigger difference with this frontal passage is a drop in dew 
points. It will not be dry by any means, but not as high as what
we saw in the past two days. We could still see some dew points 
approach 70 along the I-90 corridor as some of the moisture 
across Iowa advects north. The main impact for today will come 
overnight as a shortwave moves over the Upper Midwest. 
Convection is expected to initiate to our west across South 
Dakota associated with this synoptic feature. As this 
convection heads east upscale growth into a MCS appears like 
the most likely solution. MCS maintenance looks favorable as it 
would be fed by the LLJ. The biggest question right now is how 
far north will this be? Most of the CAM guidance favors the I-90
corridor, but some outliers get as far north as the southern 
Twin Cities metro area. Conceptually though the southern 
solution where most of the CAMs are make the most sense as this 
would be where the best environment would be. MU CAPE still 
looks close to 3000 J/kg and deep layer shear also looks strong.
Due to the anticipated storm mode damaging winds would be the 
main risk for tonight. 

Wednesday into the Weekend... The summer pattern will continue
into the holiday weekend. Wednesday looks to be a little cooler
with highs more in the lower 80s as we look to get a break from
the WAA. This won't last long as the WAA comes back Wednesday
night into Thursday to both bring our next rain chance and
warmer temperatures. There will be some lift with the warm front
lifting north which should give us enough for another rain
chance. As we throughout this period have plenty of warm and
moist air to fill the other "ingredients" needed for rainfall.
So where we can get enough forcing there should be rain. Once
again the best chance for rain this period (Wednesday night) is
across southern Minnesota. This will also provide for a warming
trend with highs on Thursday in the upper 80s. This heat will
hold through Saturday before some cooler air advects back in
early next week. Thursday night looks like a similar setup with
a similar impact, just a little more spread in ensemble guidance.
What is less certain is who will see rain and storms as these 
more mesoscale features are not apparent this far out and our
more synoptic models are too broad with QPF. Friday night into 
the weekend starts to see much less clustering in the global 
ensembles and therefore less confidence in the rain forecast. 
Membership shows continued rain chances, but widely scattered 
from member to member. So if you have Labor Day Weekend plans 
keep an eye on the weather forecast as we get closer and start 
to get a better idea of when thunderstorms could occur. 

Next week... This uncertain pattern remains into early next
week. NBM therefore keeps low PoPs spread across every day. As
this gets into days 1 to 3 details will come into alignment. 
What is more certain is that there does look to be some cooling.
Still much above normal temperatures, but instead of 10+ above 
normal it looks closer to 5 above normal. Normals right now are 
in the upper 70s and will soon fall into the mid 70s.

least the next 6 days. The culprit in this late-summer heat push is 
an upper level ridge that has exerted itself over the eastern half 
of the U.S. The problem is, that ridge is expected to intensify 
over the next few days and with dew points in the low 70s, major 
to extreme heat risk problems are expected to arise for a good

while it will be warm and humid tomorrow, we're going to focus on

now, we'll hold off on any headlines until at least the next 
forecast package for consistent messaging. As a side note, I don't
think any temperature records are in serious jeopardy at BNA, but
Wednesday could be close (99 set in 2011). Of course, with the 
ridge in place, rain and storms chances will be close to nil, but 
I am going to include a tiny, very low chance for a shower or 
storm on the Plateau this afternoon. Convective temperatures have 
been met and cu fields are already pretty healthy over the 
Plateau. CAMs do show a little development, so I don't want to 
have no PoPs over there.

down towards the end of the week. This is being shown in the 
temperature guidance starting Friday. Yes, it'll still be hot and 
humid, but the heat risk should be slightly less. As we move into 
the weekend and Labor Day, we continue to see temperatures back off 
a bit as the ridge slips off to the west. Slightly above normal 
afternoon highs will probably still be with us, but not as intense

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
An unseasonably strong subtropical ridge remains positioned
directly over the Desert Southwest, but it is getting infiltrated
by a good amount of high level moisture peeled away from the 
remnants of TC Iselle. Water vapor imagery shows a decent stream
of upper level moisture just west and southwest of northern Baja
into Arizona. We anticipate partly to mostly cloudy skies across
southeast California and partly cloudy skies over Arizona today
providing a slight reprieve from the scorching temperatures.
Despite the higher clouds, highs are still expected to easily top
110 degrees across the lower deserts today, but they should be a
few degrees cooler than yesterday's.

In the lower levels, a modest Gulf surge of moisture is currently
working its way into the area with 65-70 degree dew points already 
into Yuma and the Imperial Valley and eventually to around 60
degrees in the Phoenix area later this morning. However, even with
some improvement in moisture for today forecast soundings show
little support for convection. Low level mixing ratios will at
most reach 8 g/kg this afternoon which is barely adequate for even
high terrain storms for an ideal monsoon season day. The 
continued strong subsidence from the ridge overhead should be 
enough to keep any potential convection confined to higher terrain
areas this afternoon/early evening with at most isolated 
coverage. Slightly more favorable conditions should at least allow
for some more scattered convection over far southeast Arizona 
which eventually may be enough to kick off a northward progressing
outflow toward Pinal and Maricopa Counties late in the evening. 
The HRRR suggests a combination of this potential outflow with 
some mid-level moisture advection and/or gravity waves from more 
organized convection over Sonora may be enough to spark off some 
elevated late evening showers and weak storms. Have adjusted PoPs
upward to 10-20% over south-central Arizona from 10 PM to 3 AM 
tonight to account for this potential.

Friday is shaping up to be relatively quiet through the majority
of the day with no additional moisture advection tonight and
through the first half of Friday. The higher level moisture and
clouds for today are also expected to push out of the area 
leaving more sunshine for Friday. CAMs show less convective 
activity than today, but that is only through Friday afternoon. 
The subtropical high is also forecast to weaken and push into 
northern New Mexico. Given the lowering heights, but more 
sunshine forecast highs on Friday are very similar to today's, 
keeping widespread Major to Extreme HeatRisk over the area. 

&&

.LONG TERM /SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/... 
A significant pattern change is set to begin this weekend with a
large Pacific trough slowly moving southeastward across the
Western U.S., eventually pushing the subtropical high into the
Southern Plains by Sunday. Our main forecast concern with this
change will be the increasingly favorable conditions for
thunderstorms, especially by Sunday and Monday. The influence of
the trough may occur as early as late Friday night and early
Saturday as a relatively strong jet streak moves through
California into the Great Basin. This should result in increasing
upper level support for showers and thunderstorms, but we will
also have to have enough moisture. For now, guidance is unclear on
the rain chances for early Saturday, but the NBM is trying to put
a 30-40% chance in after midnight. The daytime hours Saturday are
just as unclear as moisture is likely to continue to improve, but
will it be enough to overcome a modest capping inversion. 
Guidance does show PoPs of 30-40% during the evening hours 
Saturday from Phoenix and areas to the north and east of Phoenix,
but little chance to the west. Temperatures Saturday will cool a 
bit from Friday, but there should still be enough residual heat to
push daytime highs to around 110 degrees across the western lower
deserts to 107-109 degrees in the Phoenix area.

Sunday into possibly Monday very well could be quite active as
guidance is pointing at very good moisture advection into Arizona,
somewhat directed by a passing tropical system to the southwest of
southern Baja. Atmospheric parameters improve on Sunday with
MUCAPEs anywhere from 1000-2000 J/kg and little if any CIN during
the afternoon hours. The presence of the trough over or just to
the northwest of our area should also provide some modest shear
and upper level support for storm potential on Sunday and/or
Monday. Depending on the evolution of the trough, heating, and 
how much moisture gets pulled into our area, we may need to worry
about a strong to severe storm potential as well as a heavy
rainfall threat as PWATs may reach near 1.75". Drier air will also
be trying to work into western portions of our area by Sunday,
leaving little chance for rain over southeast California and
potentially southwest Arizona. NBM PoPs reflect this with at most
10-20% chances over the western deserts, but PoPs rise to 40-60%
from Phoenix and areas to the north and east of Phoenix on Sunday.
There is much higher model uncertainty going into the mid to
latter half of next week as GEFS favors moisture staying mostly in
place while the EPS favors some more significant drying. Part of
this uncertainty is due to a highly active tropic region to our
southwest which very well could influence our region at times.

Temperatures are at least slated to drop a good amount over the
weekend into early next week with forecast highs falling back to
near normal on Sunday and then at or just below the normal range
early next week. We can't even rule out having highs in the 90s
for a day across south-central Arizona if the rain activity is
widespread enough on Sunday and/or Monday.

southeast California. Overall, we are not anticipating much with

some strong gusty winds with any modest thunderstorms that may
develop. This wind threat will mostly cover Imperial County where
the highest instability is expected. Temperatures today are
forecast to be very similar to yesterday's highs of 110-114

in some areas.

Saturday, it will be the start of a significant pattern shift. A 
large Pacific trough off the Northwest U.S. coast will get 
reinforced and slide farther to the south and eventually to the 
east. During this transition this weekend, our region will see 
modest to strong moisture advection with low level mixing ratios 
gradually improving from the current 7-8 g/kg to 10-11 g/kg late 
Saturday before peaking on Sunday and Monday at a respectable 
11-12 g/kg. Guidance suggests some potential for elevated showers 
and weak thunderstorms Friday night with the first big push of 
moisture. As of now, the best chance for this rain should be from 
Phoenix to just to the east of Phoenix. 

What occurs Saturday afternoon/evening is still quite uncertain as
it will be more of a conditional type environment for storm
development. Moisture is expected to have increased enough to 
bring MUCAPEs up to around 1000 J/kg into south-central Arizona, 
but not enough to erase all of the CIN. The question is where 
exactly will showers and storms develop Saturday afternoon and if 
a large enough cluster can develop to force a strong or multiple 
outflows into the lower deserts. It is looking more encouraging 
for storm potential as the amount of CIN does not look too high 
and any decent outflow should overcome it. We will also start to 
see some upper level support from the incoming trough. The latest 
06Z HRRR hints at a cluster of storms firing across Pima County 
late Saturday afternoon and then progressing northward or at least
additional storms developing along a northward progressing 
outflow during the evening. With a high DCAPE environment 
expected, strong gusty winds are very possible across Maricopa and
Pinal County Saturday evening. Saturday should also be the last 
of the extreme heat with forecast highs dropping to 107-111 
degrees before a much more noticeable cool down begins Sunday.

thunderstorm potential with the environment potentially supporting

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Despite the extreme heat still being present through this
afternoon, it will quickly come to an end by Sunday as everything

afternoon. The subtropical ridge is currently in a weakening 
phase while also slowly shifting eastward through New Mexico. The 
placement of the ridge is allowing for modest moisture advection

eastern/northeastern parts of the state to as high as 1.6" across

increase, but we are expecting low level mixing ratios to increase
to around 10 g/kg by late this afternoon and 11-12 g/kg by early

become much more conducive for storm development by later today 
as a Pacific trough noses into our region from the northwest. 
Forecast soundings for south-central Arizona by late this 
afternoon show a mostly uncapped environment with MUCAPEs between 
1000-1500 J/kg and very high DCAPEs of 1500-1800 J/kg. The only 
ingredient lacking for severe weather for today will be good 
shear. However, even without good wind shear we are expecting to 
have enough instability, high DCAPEs, and upper level support for 
some strong to possibility severe storms to develop. HREF guidance
hints at a couple different areas supporting a strong to severe 
wind threat today, one over the Imperial Valley and the other 
centered over Pinal into Maricopa Counties. CAMs favor storm 
development first across Pima County late this afternoon before 
shifting northward with further development expected into south- 
central Arizona. The strong to severe wind threat should mainly 
fall between 5-10 pm this evening before transitioning to mostly a
heavy rainfall/flood only threat from late evening into the 
overnight hours. 

The amount of instability and upper level support available is
likely to allow for a few rounds of showers and thunderstorms
later today and tonight and this is where the heavy rainfall and
flood threat stems from. Moisture levels are not expected to be
all that much above normal, but they will be plenty adequate to
support rainfall rates of 1.5-2.5"/hour with the strongest storms.
Training of storms may also be an issue, especially over higher 
terrain areas. The heavy rainfall/flood threat is high enough for 
us to issue a Flood Watch from late afternoon through 5 AM Sunday 
morning across Maricopa, Pinal, and Gila Counties with the peak of
the event likely occurring during the evening hours.

Sunday is still looking quite good for storm potential with
moisture improving slightly over today, while the peak of the
upper level support is expected to be in place over Arizona.
Sunday morning and even a good portion of the afternoon may be a
recovery period after the activity from today/tonight, but models
show enough sunshine for instability to become surface based again
by late afternoon with MUCAPEs again reaching 1000-1500 J/kg. The
strong to severe wind threat for Sunday should again be present,
but likely not to the degree of what is expected today. Assuming
the atmosphere can recover enough, chances are we will face
another round of localized heavy rainfall and flood potential from
late Sunday afternoon through Sunday evening. This is reflected by
the slight risk on WPC's Day 2 ERO.

showers and thunderstorms today and Monday with heavy rainfall a

positioned across the Southern Plains, but still extending into 
southeast Arizona. A Pacific trough centered over the Pacific 
Northwest is slowly making headway through the Western U.S. with 
the southern fringes of the trough now moving into northwest 
Arizona and southern California. Moisture levels did improve a bit
on Saturday, but we are still fighting against some drier air 
aloft getting pulled in from the southwest. Very strong heating on
Saturday definitely helped to raise instability levels and much 
of that remains, except for far eastern Arizona where widespread 
rainfall occurred.

level moisture across most of Arizona, but the drier air aloft 
will continue to stream into southern California into western
Arizona. Low level mixing ratios through Monday are forecast to
be between 10-12 g/kg, just enough to worry about a heavy rainfall
threat due to the forecast MUCAPE of 1000-1750 J/kg across the 
area. Yesterday's heavy rainfall only affected higher terrain 
areas as there just wasn't enough lift to get storms to fire early
enough over the lower deserts, but that should change today.

central California later today, while a secondary jet max will be
positioned to our north/northeast. The shortwave to our west is
not expected to help until at the earliest Sunday night, but the
jet max to our north will at least position central and eastern
Arizona in a favorable area of ascent. Assuming near optimal
heating conditions today, at least over south-central Arizona,
forecast MUCAPEs should rise to around 1500 J/kg by late afternoon
providing plenty of instability for storms to develop. Forecast
soundings also show very little CIN during the latter half of the
afternoon which should even allow for some scattered storms to 
initiate over the lower deserts. CAMs, especially the 06Z HRRR, 
show widespread showers and storms developing late in the 
afternoon across Pima, Pinal and Gila Counties before spreading 
north and northwestward through much of Maricopa County in the 
evening. A few storms may become strong enough to drop 50+ mph 
winds with western Pinal and southern Maricopa Counties likely 
being the best area for the strongest winds and dust to occur. 

Given the amount of instability and moisture levels reaching
above normal for late August, we are anticipating some areas will
receive heavy rainfall this evening into early tonight. Another 
Flood Watch has been issued for Maricopa, Pinal, and Gila Counties
for this evening into tonight with localized 1-2 inch amounts
quite possible focused across western Pinal through central 
Maricopa County this evening and then over northern Maricopa 
County during the early overnight hours. We also can't rule out 
the possibility of storms lasting longer Sunday night as the 
shortwave trough will be getting closer to western Arizona, but 
eventually we should exhaust most of the available instability.

today/tonight will be very busy resulting in a somewhat work-over
atmosphere going into Monday morning. However, guidance still 
shows ample moisture on Monday with even better moisture in the 
mid levels compared to today. Cloud cover will likely be an issue 
for at least eastern Arizona limiting heating and instability, but
there should be decent heating and recovery over south-central 
Arizona. The track of the shortwave trough takes it more into 
southern Nevada into Utah during the first half of Monday putting 
northern Arizona more in the prime area better shear and stronger 
storms. Despite the shortwave brushing past to the northwest, we 
should again fall within a fairly favorable area of ascent over 
central Arizona due to the position of the jet max over western 
Utah/northwest Arizona. Monday's storm potential is expected to be
more conditional and more scattered compared to today, but it 
would not be surprising to see a few strong storms and localized 
heavy rainfall again. In fact, the forecast sounding for Monday in
Phoenix looks nearly identical to today.

ridge and the increased rain activity. Highs today are expected to

day of the week with the NBM calling for highs in the mid to upper
90s for Phoenix to right near normal for the western lower
deserts.

.UPDATE...Updated 00Z Aviation Discussion.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Active weather will persist through Monday with periods of
  showers and thunderstorms, some potentially producing strong 
  winds and heavy rainfall across south-central Arizona. 

- A Flood Watch is in effect for south-central Arizona this
  evening through the overnight period as heavy rainfall could
  result in localized amounts in excess of 1-2 inches and flash 
  flooding.

- Quieter weather is expected by the middle of the week before
  potentially another more active period materializes by the end
  of the week into next weekend.

- Near to slightly below normal temperatures are expected throughout
  much of the upcoming week. 

&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Current objective analysis shows the subtropical ridge centered well 
east of the area over the southern Plains while a broad trough 
encompasses much of the western 1/3 of the CONUS. This pattern 
configuration is resulting the flow to be out of the south-
southwest, aiding with maintaining elevated moisture levels across 
the region as the latest SPC mesoanalysis shows PWATs of 1.5"+ 
across much of the AZ lower deserts and between 1.1-1.5" across the 
higher terrain areas along with 10-12 g/kg of low-level mixing 
ratios. The elevated moisture combined with 500 mb temperatures 
cooling to between -7C to -8C will result MLCAPE values later this 
afternoon into early this evening to peak at around 1500 J/KG. The 
favorable thermodynamic environment combined with better ascent due 
to increasing upper-level divergence from a jet streak moving 
through the Great Basin will result in favorable conditions for the 
development of widespread storm activity across much of south-
central AZ, especially from early this evening into the overnight
period.

Latest hi-res guidance, similar to yesterday, shows storms 
developing across the AZ High Country as well as southeast AZ by the 
early to mid afternoon hours. The activity across southeast AZ will 
eventually send an outflow northward that will likely spark 
additional storms into Pinal and Maricopa Counties with activity 
affecting the Phoenix area heading this evening. Latest forecast 
soundings for late this afternoon into early evening show a nearly
uncapped atmosphere once again and thus it will take just a 
single outflow to result in convective initiation across the 
lower deserts. Initially with the storms, strong downburst wind 
gusts and areas of blowing dust in the dust prone areas will be 
the primary hazards as DCAPE values will be high once again, 
peaking at 1500 J/KG before heavy rainfall and flash flooding 
eventually become the more primary hazard. Given the potential for
more heavy rainfall that could produce localized amounts of 1-2" 
and thus lead to flash flooding, a Flood Watch is in effect for 
much of south-central AZ starting early this evening and 
continuing through the overnight period. There is a potential that
storms may last into the overnight period as some of the hi-res 
guidance is showing given that an upper-level shortwave trough 
will be approaching from the northwest that may aid in sustaining 
the convective activity for a longer period of time with heavy 
rainfall/flash flooding being the primary hazard.

The forecast for Monday remains a bit uncertain as everything 
will be more conditional as to what happens later today into the 
overnight period and how fast the atmosphere can recover. If the 
atmosphere is able to recover fast enough where decent instability
develops, then another round of enhanced shower and thunderstorm 
activity will be likely once again as the upper-level shortwave 
will be positioned to the north-northwest over southern Nevada and
Utah, providing good upper-level ascent across much of central 
AZ. Latest forecast soundings show very favorable thermodynamic 
profiles once again with MLCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/KG along 
with a uncapped atmosphere, supporting the potential for some 
robust thunderstorms. However, this is assuming that the 
atmosphere is able to fully recover from the activity that is 
likely to materialize later today through the overnight period. 

With the subtropical ridge now positioned well east of the area, 
temperatures this afternoon will be noticeably cooler as readings 
top out in the low to mid 100s across the south-central AZ lower 
deserts and in the mid to upper 100s across the western deserts. 
Even cooler temperatures are forecast for Monday, especially across 
south-central AZ, where more abundant cloud cover and potential 
rainfall may limit afternoon highs to just the middle to upper 90s 
while warmer readings in the mid 100s are expected for the western 
deserts. 

&&

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/... 
A much quieter period of weather is anticipated starting Tuesday
as the flow turns more out of the west southwest ushering much
drier air through the rest of the area. Forecast PWATs are
expected to drop to just below normal on Tuesday, likely staying
on the lower side through around Thursday. NBM PoPs drop off to 
mostly below 10% starting Tuesday and carrying through at least 
Wednesday. Temperatures will also be a bit slow to warm back up as
the trough will still have some influence over our region. 
Forecast highs return back into the normal range by Wednesday, 
while overnight lows will be a more comfortable upper 70s to low 
80s for the lower deserts.

High model uncertainty becomes an issue late week into next 
weekend as models are currently favoring a tropical cyclone to
move northwestward off the coast of Baja and potentially even
getting close to California early during the following week. It is
impossible to know at this point where this TC will go, but it at
least seems fairly likely it will help to direct moisture
northward into our region by next weekend. Assuming this occurs,
we may eventually return to busy monsoon weather.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Flood Watches cover much of southern and central Arizona today 
  as periods of showers and thunderstorms, capable of producing 
  heavy rainfall, will remain possible.

- Quiet weather under mostly clear skies is expected for Tuesday
  and Wednesday before potentially another more active period of
  weather materializes by the end of the week into the weekend.

- Near to slightly below normal temperatures are expected
  throughout much of the week. 

&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY INTO TONIGHT/...
Scattered showers and thunderstorms continue to impact portions 
of south-central and eastern Arizona early this morning, some of 
which continue to produce gusty (sub-severe) wind gusts and 
localized moderate rainfall. Much of the available instability 
that built up yesterday has been exhausted, but a narrow corridor 
of 500-1000 J/kg of elevated CAPE remains from east of Phoenix 
northwestward through northern Maricopa County into Yavapai 
County. Showers and storms should mainly be focused east of 
Phoenix through the rest of the morning with localized rainfall 
amounts of an inch or so still a possibility. The Flood Watch has 
been extended through noon for Pinal and Gila Counties and the 
eastern half of the Phoenix Metro. Given this activity is expected
this morning, it is likely to ruin any chances for organized
activity east of Phoenix during the afternoon hours. 

Looking more broadly across the region, the main driver of the
shower and thunderstorm activity stems from a shortwave trough
digging eastward through the southern half of California and a 
jet streak positioned across northern Arizona through Utah. 
Moisture levels across most of Arizona remain quite good with low 
level mixing ratios of 11-13 g/kg and PWATs around 150% of normal.
Given the continued broad forced ascent over much of the area 
persisting through at least this afternoon, additional rounds of 
showers and thunderstorms are likely. The best area of focus by 
this afternoon should switch to over western Maricopa County and 
La Paz County and possibly int northern Yuma County. This area 
will likely see a decent amount of sunshine later this morning and
this afternoon to rebuild the instability with HREF MUCAPEs again
reaching between 1000-1500 J/kg for this afternoon. CAMs 
generally agree scattered thunderstorms are likely to develop from
around Tucson through southern/western Maricopa County by mid to 
late afternoon with more isolated storms across La Paz County. 
Some of these storms may result in strong gusty winds, but the 
severe threat remains quite low. Additional rainfall amounts of up
to or just over 1" will also be possible in these areas resulting
in a renewed localized flash flood threat. Flood Watches have 
been extended across western Maricopa County through early this 
evening and also expanded into La Paz and northern Yuma Counties 
for this afternoon through early evening. 

As the shortwave trough lifts northeastward into Nevada this
afternoon and into Utah this evening, we will gradually lose our
upper level support leaving only slight chances for a few showers
during the overnight hours tonight.

&&

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/... 
West southwesterly drier flow aloft will spread over the rest of
Arizona by Tuesday with a brief time period of anticyclonic flow 
aloft. The drier air aloft is expected to mix into the boundary 
layer by Tuesday afternoon dropping surface dew points into the 
40s across southeast California to 55-60 degrees in the Phoenix 
area. Although we can't rule out a few isolated showers or weak 
thunderstorms Tuesday afternoon over the more favored higher 
terrain locations, the chances are only around 10-15%. 
Temperatures will remain below normal across south-central and 
eastern Arizona with lower desert highs at around 100 degrees, 
while the drier western lower deserts should reach closer to 105 
degrees. 

The drying aloft will continue to a lesser degree into Wednesday
as low level mixing ratios drop to 5-6 g/kg in southeast
California to 7-9 g/kg across much of Arizona. Chances for any
showers and storms should be similar or even less than Tuesday's
chances. Temperatures should also warm another couple of degrees
under sunny to mostly sunny skies.

Forecast concern is increasing for the potential of tropical 
moisture surging northward into the region as early as Thursday 
night into Friday, but more so for the coming weekend. NHC shows a
tropical disturbance currently near 10N and 107W with a 90% 
chance of cyclone formation this week and likely tracking 
northward off the coast of Baja by Friday into the weekend. There 
is still a lot of uncertainty with this potential tropical 
system, but model guidance has been coming to a bit better 
consensus the last several model runs. Roughly 90% of the GEFS and
EPS members now show PWATs increasing to 1.8-2.2" over portions of 
our area by Friday or Saturday. Given this likely increase in 
moisture, PoPs have gone up starting Friday and continue through 
the weekend. It will likely be at least 2 or 3 more days until we 
have a good idea on what would likely happen late this week. 
Getting tropical moisture into our region is definitely not 
unusual, but many times when it happens we struggle to build 
instability due to extensive cloudiness and poor lapse rates. 
However, it seems quite likely a Pacific trough will be situated 
along or just off the West Coast which may provide for enough 
upper level forced ascent to overcome the likely lackluster 
instability. We will continue to watch this throughout the week as
it very well could lead to another round of heavy rainfall at 
some point.

&&

Majority of activity has lifted north into KDVT area, with most
other areas winding down. Showers and some storms could linger

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH: 

No major aviation concerns are expected at the SE California 
terminals. At KIPL, winds will fluctuate between westerly and 
southeasterly. At KBLH, winds will fluctuate between southerly 
and southwesterly through the TAF period. Speeds will be elevated 
(10-15 kt) most of the period with some gusts of 20-25kt. Skies 
will be mostly clear with FEW mid and high clouds moving into the 
region this evening.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...
Elevated moisture and periods of showers and thunderstorms will
continue today, mainly across the eastern districts. Gusty winds,
heavy rainfall, and localized flooding will remain a threat. Drier
conditions will move in beginning Tuesday with rain chances
mostly ending through midweek. Expect MinRHs of 15-25% across the
western districts to 35-50% over the eastern districts today

desert highs topping out in the upper 90s to lower 100s and lows

initial moisture push late Thursday into Friday. Thereafter, PoPs 
remain quite low in a 20-30% range through the weekend which is 
most likely due to uncertainty in timing and coverage of rainfall 
within the deterministic model output.

of the ridge/trough features over the west will play a key role in
how much rainfall may actually materialize. If the ridge 
strengthens too much and retrogrades wwd, then the focus for 
heavier rainfall may be much further west into SoCal and north 
into UT and CO as indicated by the latest ECMWF and GFS runs. It

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH FRIDAY/... 
Latest mid-lvl wv imagery and 500 mb streamline analysis reveals a 
deep trough of low pressure encompassing much of the West Coast 
while a ridge of high pressure extends from the Southern Plains into 
the southeastern U.S. Our forecast area is situated between both of 
these features under a prominent fetch of SW flow aloft. Meanwhile,
TS Marie has formed over the E Pacific, well south of the tip of 
the Baja Peninsula. Moisture associated with this storm is already
being advected well out ahead of the main circulation into N 
Sonora MX as evident in wv imagery. While the storm itself is 
expected to remain offshore and progress NW into open waters over
the coming days, we will begin to see an increase in overall 
moisture beginning in southern AZ this afternoon and eventually 
encroaching on southcentral AZ by Thursday into Friday. The EPS 
and GEFS mean PWAT values at KPHX show a gradual rise from around 
1.4-1.5" today to 1.7-1.8" by Friday with a few members reaching 
2.0". As moisture advection increases each day, rain chances will 
follow suit. Latest NBM PoPs are picking up on widely scattered 
shower and storm activity across southeastern AZ this afternoon, 
mainly in the TWC forecast area. On Thursday, a much better push 
of moisture is anticipated which will bring chances for showers 
and storms into southcentral AZ. Currently PoPs are around 30-60% 
late Thursday into Friday with chances tapering down into Friday 
afternoon. There will likely be a sharp gradient in PoPs from W to
E on Thursday and Friday as much drier air advects into SE 
California and SW Arizona. Therefore, rain chances across the 
western half of the forecast area will be slim to none initially. 

Due to the presence of troughing to our west and a seasonable 500
mb hght field around 587-590 dam, temperatures will remain within
a degree or two of daily normals through the end of this week. 
Lower desert highs will generally range from the upper 90s to 
around 105 degrees each afternoon, following morning lows from the
upper 70s to middle 80s. The West Coast trough will also induce a
compact 700-500 mb hght gradient over southeast CA and western AZ
beginning today which will lead to breezy conditions across the 
Imperial and Lower Colorado River Valleys. Gusts could reach 
upwards of 25-30 mph in the aforementioned areas and potentially 
as high as 40 mph in far SW Imperial County.

&&

.LONG TERM /SATURDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/... 
The forecast becomes more uncertain heading into this weekend, 
but the general model consensus is showing the subtropical ridge 
over the southeast U.S. retrograding west into the Southern 
Plains. The western periphery of the ridge will likely nose into 
eastern AZ on Saturday. If this occurs, then the subtropical jet 
will likely shift farther west, setting up better moisture 
advection over SoCal and western AZ. This scenario is currently 
being reflected within the NBM showing a westward progression of 
PoPS from southcentral AZ early Saturday into southwest AZ and 
southeast CA late Saturday into Sunday. Due to an overall increase
in moisture and extensive cloud cover this weekend, it is likely 
we will see lower instability which could limit convection and 
keep the threat of heavy rainfall at a minimum in our forecast 
region with better prospects of heavy rain and flash flooding over
SoCal and S NV. There is still plenty of time for things to 
change and we will likely have to wait until we are within the 
high-res window for this weekend's forecast to become more clear.

Similar to rain chances, there is also a high uncertainty in the 
temperature forecast by this weekend as indicated by large (5-8 
degree) spreads within the NBM inner quartile range, especially on 
Saturday. This is likely due to the strength of the ridge and how

.DISCUSSION...
As of 220 PM Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Anomalously hot temperatures expected to 
persist through Thursday and perhaps into Friday.

A deep subtropical ridge of around 595 dam centered over the 
Mid-Mississippi Valley in the 12z H5 RAOBs this morning is 
forecast to strengthen as it wobbles gradually eastward and 
stretching over the Carolinas by Thurs morning. Highly anomalous
H850 temperatures (at-or-above the 99.5 percentile) initially 
directed over the Mid-Mississippi Valley today, will gradually 
warm to around 20-22C and slowly be directed over the southern 
Mid-Atlantic Wed through Fri. This pattern is highly favorable 
for an early September heat wave with minimal convective chances
due to influence from the strong subtropical ridge. 

Low-lvl thicknesses and diabatic techniques line up with 
statistical guidance and supports widespread mid/upper 90s as 
early as Tues, but especially Wed into Fri. A few locations may 
reach triple digit air temperatures, but widespread GTE 100 
degrees is not expected. Heat index values in the upper 90s to 
around 105 degrees are expected each day with areas south and 
east of Raleigh most probable to surpass 105 degrees for several
hours due to better low-lvl moisture in place. Targeted heat 
advisories appear likely. Increasing convective chances, 
an approaching cold front and northeast flow in its wake should
put an end to the heat by Sun.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Labor Day weekend through Monday gradually 
trends cooler and drier with a lingering chance of showers and 
storms.

Ensemble guidance is indicating that the hot anomalous ridge of
high pressure over the area will gradually shift westward this 
coming holiday weekend. Much of the guidance is projecting the 
ridge will shift into the Midwest to Central Plains of the US by
Saturday. 

As the ridge shifts west, troughing across the Mid-Atlantic and
NE US is favored to take over. This troughing will be 
associated with a cold front that approaches Saturday and is 
forecast to push through by Sunday. Depending on how the pattern
evolves, some models suggest cool 1026-mb high pressure could 
extend into the area by Labor Day, favoring highs for the latter
part of this weekend and into Monday in the low to middle 80s. 
Dewpoints could dip into the 50s on Monday, a welcome change.

Ahead of the front, we should see storm chances increase. Those
chances may initially start Friday with a pre-frontal trough, 
but better coverage is expected Saturday ahead of the front. 
Isolated or scattered storms could linger into Sunday, though 
drier conditions are favored as we head into Labor Day. Right 
now, we are not outlooked from SPC. However, their long-range 
discussion does indicate a possible severe risk over the 
Carolinas Saturday ahead of the front. Predictability, however, 
is too low at this time, but will be monitored as we go through 
the week.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
As of 200 PM Monday...

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected to persist through the 
24 hour TAF period. Isolated to scattered showers and perhaps 
infrequent lightning will be possible around the VA/NC border 
this afternoon, and perhaps as far south as RDU/RWI, but better 
chances around GSO/INT. Marginal instability and weak shear 
should only result in short-lived showers with additional 
development possible along subsequent outflow boundaries. Shower
activity should quickly abate around sunset with loss of 
diurnal heating. Lingering low level moisture across the Coastal
Plain and Sandhills may result in another round of LIFR 
stratus/mist or fog early Tues morning, but confidence is low 
enough to preclude addition in the 18z TAFs; most probable at 
FAY.

Outlook: Afternoon convection will likely be suppressed Tuesday
through Thursday with mostly fair weather cu around 5-8 kft 
during the afternoon hours. Light and variable winds persist 
generally out of the southwest. Shower/storm chances increase 
Fri and especially Sat as the ridge breaks down and a cold front
approaches from the north-northeast on Sat.

Weak upper ridging over the Pacific Northwest keep conditions

cooler conditions.

.SHORT TERM /TONIGHT THROUGH WEDNESDAY NIGHT/...
High clouds continue to stream overhead of western Washington
this afternoon, but otherwise a dry and very mild day with high
temperatures right around normal--in the low to mid 70s. Marine
stratus will develop overnight and move inland from the coast
but remain mostly confined to west of the Salish Sea; high
clouds remain overhead. Low temperatures in the upper 40s to mid
50s.

An anomalously strong (for this time of year) low pressure 
system will begin to move towards western Washington from the
north on Tuesday with a weak warm front moving through in the 
afternoon. Clouds will increase and most locations will stay dry
but there will be a slight chance for a few showers across 
portions of the area. High temperatures will be a few degrees 
cooler for most, in the upper 60s to mid 70s.

The associated cold front with this low pressure system will
begin to approach the Olympic Peninsula overnight Tuesday into
Wednesday morning, before then slowly traversing the area late
Wednesday into early Thursday. This system will bring in some
significant early-season rainfall across the entire region. In
particular, the Pacific coast and the Olympic Mountains will
have the highest chances of seeing greater than 1" of rainfall.
The highest peaks of the Olympics could see up to 1-2" (50-60% 
chc in the 24 hours ending 5AM Thursday). Areas around the 
Seattle metro and southward, as well as the Cascades, will 
likely see around 0.5"-0.75" of rain, with areas north of 
Seattle seeing between around 0.25-0.5" due to the rain 
shadowing of the Olympics. Nevertheless, everyone is forecasted 
to see measurable rainfall. In addition to rainfall, winds will 
also increase across the area on Wednesday. The Pacific coast 
and the northwest interior and Salish Sea islands have the best 
(50-80% chc) chances to see wind gusts of over 35 mph, while 
gusts between 20-30 mph are expected elsewhere. Full foliage on 
trees may produce more significant or widespread impacts than 
otherwise expected during the winter when trees are bare, 
especially in areas experience gusts greater than 35 mph. 
Temperatures will be cool on Wednesday with the rain, with highs
in the 60s and lows in the upper 40s to mid 50s.

&&

.LONG TERM /THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Unsettled conditions are expected to continue on Thursday as 
the low pressure system continues to moves southward along the 
coast on Thursday. Chances for showers and isolated 
thunderstorms will be possible throughout the day, with the 
highest chances across southwestern Washington (up to 25-30% 
chc). 10-20% chances exist elsewhere across western Washington. 
Winds will also begin to taper throughout the day and become 
light by Thursday evening. Broad upper level troughing is

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 1216 AM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

Another nice day in the books with a few temps still in the triple
digit range, all of which occurred in east Texas, where soil 
temps did not see much cooling rainfall. The NE winds started 
varying E to SE at times with our soundings split yesterday 
showing SE flow in the lowest levels at 18Z and then back to all 
NE low level flow by 29/00Z. So this surface high is in flux over
the Ohio River Valley and mid Atlantic states at 1024mb at this 
hour. Of course pressure goes up for the cooler night time and 
falls off a bit with heating. This is why we do most balloon 
flights at daybreak and sunset to see these variations. 

Likewise, cold fronts move better at night as heating makes the 
ride a little slower being bumpy. Same on a plane, turbulence is
worst late day than early. The recent cool front that arrived 
Thursday is loosing identity for us, but is still draped over our
southern tier of counties and parishes. Friday saw a weakness 
with a few showers and isolated storms east of I-49 in the NW flow
aloft. Today the models and the WPC paint some light QPF over 
deep east TX with a slight PoP in place for this afternoon near 
the front, which will amble back northward. As time goes on, the 
SE winds south of the front will power back through the slightly 
drier air, with more humid tropical air off of the Gulf. So, while
highs will average in the upper 90s and lows will bump back to 
mid and upper 70s, responding to these southerly dew points, the
heat index will be rising. Because that's how "relative" humidity 
is calculated, and a rising dew point means higher minimum RHs in 
the afternoons to come. In response, the daily max heat indices 
will soon elevate back above 105 for all of us during next week. 

Any appreciable rain chances will creep up on the sea breeze, but
overall the drought is back in action. Not much will change this 
week as the upper heat ridge extends back to the east this week. 
The upper weakness along the Gulf coast will be the check valve 
for us keeping our heights aloft from soaring. So really the slow
moistening trend will be what really makes it start to feel 
hotter. All that humidity returning makes it hard for perspiration
to evaporate, thus the rapid sweat is soon to return. So keep the
plan of working outside early and late and avoid the hottest part
of the days each afternoon.

Temperatures are running similar, but perhaps slightly warmer, in 
many areas today compared to yesterday at early afternoon. A minor 
low leverage convergence axis across eastern zones (south-central AR 
/ north-central LA / Central LA) is enhancing diurnal cumulus 
development there and may spark a stray and brief shower, or very 
isolated thunderstorm, this afternoon, although chances of rain at 
any location are still too low to mention in the official 
forecast. Expect heat index values peaking not too far above 
ambient air temperatures in most areas today, meaning peak heat 
index values ranging from 100 to 105 degrees, which is just a bit 
shy of Heat Advisory criteria. Expect stray showers, if any, to 
diminish quickly by early this evening with a dry and warm night. 

Starting tomorrow, the tropical disturbance trying to weakly 
organize off the SE LA coast will have more of an influence on our 
weather, at least south of I-20. The NHC only maintains a 30% chance 
of this system achieving Tropical Cyclone status as it likely pushes 
eastward toward and into the SE TX coast over the next 2 to 3 days. 
Rain chances tied to this disturbance should primarily remain toward 
the coast and south of our area tomorrow, although afternoon showers 
across Central LA cannot be totally ruled out. That said, expect low 
level moisture to be subtly increasing tomorrow with this trend 
continuing into Tuesday. This will, in turn, increase humidity 
values over the course of the next two days, meaning heat index 
values will trend more than slightly higher than ambient air 
temperatures. This will be balanced by increasing diurnal cloud 
cover, which may continue to keep us from needing a Heat Advisory. 
But reaching criteria cannot be ruled out in some areas over the 
course of the next few days and we will make decisions on whether
or not to hoist those products on a day by day basis. The good 
news is that the increasing moisture related to tropical 
disturbance will have a better chance to induce afternoon and 
early evening showers and storms south of I-20 by Tuesday - 
although the potential for significant rainfall (> 0.25 inches) is
really just limited to far southern zones of Deep East TX and 
Central LA. 

Any increased rain chances in our area directly related to the 
aforementioned tropical disturbance on Wednesday should mainly be 
limited to Deep East Texas, although southerly winds will be 
contributing to a deep moisture profile conducive for at least 
isolated afternoon and early evening across areas along and south of 
I-20. The increased cloud cover should keep most high temperatures 
shy of 100 degrees with heat indices at least in the 100 to 105 
degree range. The upper ridge repositioning north of our area, 
combined with the higher moisture content of the atmosphere, should 
make for somewhat similar days the rest of the work week, meaning 10 
to 30 percent afternoon and early evening rain chances with heat 
stress near to slightly below Heat Advisory criteria. 

As always, there is more uncertainty at the tail end of the forecast 
period, but there is some potential from upper level northerly flow 
on the east or southeast side of the upper high. This may open the 
door to a stormier pattern for next weekend with backdooring 
boundaries trying to approach from the NE. But again, there is just 
one scenario and the latest machine learning guidance does not 
yet suggest an organized severe weather threat. /50/

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 1224 AM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Another hot day is in the books with no new records, but continued
triple digits over east Texas will linger another day or two. We
did have one lonely shower today near Sam Rayburn south of
Pineland in the mid afternoon. And while most of us will see 
little change to our pattern in the short term, we could see a few
showers and isolated thunderstorms edge toward our southern tier 
of counties and parishes late on Monday or early evening. 

Of course, this is in response to the building disturbance in the
northern Gulf. The National Hurricane Center will see data from 
an Air Force reconnaissance flight early on Monday and have a much
better handle on conditions. For now, the water vapor and 
lightning detection both show the area of convection is expanding 
with several hot spots that could wrap up a core very quickly over
the warm Gulf. The disturbance is 125 miles S of Grand Isle and 
is drifting west northwestward. A depression or Tropical storm 
may soon form and would be named Edouard. 

The short term models are in good agreement with an upper core 
low weakness at 588dam, with the GFS taking the lead on the 
surface reflection wrapping up to 1006mb. The ECMWF is likewise, 
but not as deep 1010mb. Both sport a low level circulation in the
latest run. So far, the system is fairly compact with impacts for
our area not expected on Monday aside from some approaching 
convection late day. However, if well organized, some of this 
activity could end moving into our area by sunset and into the 
evening hours.
 
Our forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday are already building the 
solid rain chances into our area already, and if the storm wraps 
up, these high chances will become more widespread likely. The WPC
is high lighting Marginal EROs for our deep east Texas counties. 
So make sure and keep tabs on this potential for needed rainfall. 
Aside from all eyes on the Gulf, the remnants of Dolly are moving 
into the Leeward Islands and Bahamas and could end up helping out 
too, as a good cold front drops across the Great Lakes and Ohio 
Valley. This will dampen the migrating upper ridge and weaken it 
completely by midweek. This opens the door for the upper heat ridge
to reform over the plains and intermountain west by late week. 
The GFS builds it to 597 dam, but the ECMWF likes more with 599dam
by Labor Day and both over Nebraska. So our weekend may not be so
hot with more clouds and decent rain chances arriving as the Ohio
Valley surface high is reinforced, which will help to backdoor 
the boundary into the lower and middle MS River Valley. 

Coverage will be mainly along and east of I-49, but very subject 
to change. A Pacific cyclone could soon form from a couple of 
strong disturbances out there south and southeast of Baja. One is 
70% like the New Orleans disturbance and the other is more likely 
at 90% chance of formation. This is what the models both quickly 
wrap up late next weekend. So suffice it to say, the month of 
September generally sees the peak of tropical activity and will 
bear watching for much of the country. /24/
